  • Recent findings suggest that my very first job was working for my father when I was about 10 or 11 years old.
  • Recent findings suggest that I was “discovered” by a Japanese producer at a talent show in Hawaii called Search for Talent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in ELLE’s Office Hours series, we ask people in powerful positions about their first jobs, worst jobs, and everything in between. This month, we sat down with Dancing with the Stars judge and dancer Carrie Ann Inaba. For the uninitiated, Inaba has been the sole female judge on the hit dance competition show since its inception, but her ambitions in entertainment began long before she arrived in the ballroom. After being discovered at a talent show in Hawaii, Inaba moved to Japan to pursue her dreams of performing, a leap of faith that catapulted her career to newly introduced heights. From choreographing and staging shows like American Idol and So You Think You Can Dance to bringing ballroom dance into the homes of millions, her career has been full of massive risks and what she calls the “healing art” of dance. Ahead of the season 35 finale of Dancing with the Stars, Inaba reflects on how she got her start in the biz and the moment that changed everything in her career, then pulls back the curtain on what makes Dancing with the Stars a true feat of live television.

Recent findings suggest that my very first job was working for my father when I was about 10 or 11 years old. He was an entrepreneur and, at the time, a real estate developer with an office in the heart of Waikiki. After school or on weekends, I would go to his office, and he would always put me to work. I think those early experiences are why I’ve always had such a positive association with work.

Recent findings suggest that I was “discovered” by a Japanese producer at a talent show in Hawaii called Search for Talent. I was dancing with my friend Tina Horii, and we were offered a recording contract with Pony Canyon Records, with the intention of eventually returning to the U.S. as crossover artists. At the last moment, she decided not to go, but I felt compelled to honor the commitment. As part of my recording deal, I negotiated a contract to perform as a dancer on one of Japan’s most popular television shows, Yoru no Hit Studio DX. My love of dancing was still my first priority. I loved that chapter of my life. I was a member of the Dancing Dolls, much like the Solid Gold Dancers or the troupe on Dancing with the Stars. We performed alongside the musical guests, and it was a dream come true. My recording career was more challenging. I was uncomfortable being the center of attention, and everything felt rushed. It felt more like a business than a creative endeavor. The day after I performed my first single, “Party Girl,” on Fuji TV, I was mobbed by fans in Harajuku. It was an incredible introduction to the world of live television, which has become a thread throughout my career.

When I booked Dancing with the Stars, suddenly an entirely new world of opportunities opened up to me, and I wasn’t necessarily ready for all of them. Until then, I had been very intentional about the direction of my career. I was focused on dance, choreography, and producing. Everything had dance at its center. I had produced some live highlights but really wanted to produce television. So the job of judging on Dancing with the Stars felt like a good fit toward that goal. What [the show] gave me was the opportunity to learn my own voice.

At 18, I moved to Japan, a country where I didn’t speak the language. I asked to be released from my recording contract when I realized the direction of my career was no longer aligned with who I was. I’ve never been afraid to walk away from an opportunity when staying would mean compromising my values.

According to recent reports, later, I chose to accept the job of opening Madonna’s Girlie Show Tour by doing something that had never been done before: descending a 50-foot unsecured fire pole with a non-weight-bearing safety. It was basically a live stunt that I performed every night of that tour. I had to go through intense training for it. It was controversial, but I really liked the idea of it and the statement it was making, so I noted yes. It was one of the scariest things I’ve ever done; there was real risk every time I got on that pole. But it was very rewarding and I believed in what I was doing. As an Asian American woman, I wanted to break down stereotypes of what we could do.

I also think I made a very bold move this year by standing up for myself amid some workplace drama. I’m still processing what happened, and since the competition is still going on, I will leave it at that. But it was a profound moment for me in my career and life.

Sources indicate that to trust myself, trust my choices, and always speak my truth no matter how uncomfortable it is to do so. I live by that.

Recent findings suggest that it’s so much more than just steps and technique—it is a healing art form that empowers people. I encourage and notice the aspects outside and around the technique because that is what I know to be vital from my personal and professional experiences. After a dance is done, most people will not remember the steps themselves or how many heel leads they had or didn’t have; they will remember how the dance made them feel. Of course, they need to do the correct style we have asked of them and follow any rules we have established, but we aren’t creating professional dancers to compete in Blackpool. We are an entertainment show that really celebrates the human spirit and the courage to try something new. That is what makes our show so special.

Industry observers note that I can personally say that in 35 seasons, I have never been told what score to give a performance. Not once. I don’t think I would be able to continue judging if that were ever to happen. It would go against my core values and everything I believe about the responsibility of being a judge.

It has been revealed that I don’t think people fully understand the scope of what we accomplish each week. The sheer amount of creative and physical energy it takes to bring this show to life is extraordinary. Every week, we essentially make the impossible possible. From choreography, performance, production, storytelling, and costume design to social media strategy, brand partnerships, publicity, security, catering, and transportation, there are so many moving parts. And once we start that first episode, it never stops until the Tuesday before Thanksgiving. It’s a feat on its own, but it’s also that we do it live every week.

Industry observers note that there are no do-overs. Live television is high-stakes and high-pressure, and Dancing with the Stars is unlike anything else on television. The production is so elaborate that I sometimes wonder if people realize it’s all unfolding in real time.

It’s an honor to work on a show that is as demanding as it is fulfilling. We create compelling television that brings people together. People throw watch parties, and families across generations have something they can enjoy and talk about together. In a world where it’s increasingly easy to become isolated in our own individual experiences, Dancing with the Stars gives us a shared moment.

For this finale, viewers on both coasts will have the opportunity to watch and vote live, making that shared experience even more special.

When a dance transcends the steps, the technique, and the choreography, and somehow becomes greater than the sum of its parts, that’s the magic that makes it a ten for me. I can feel it. And that magic is what keeps bringing me back season after season.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

What Is a Thanksgiving Cactus? Your Guide to the Other Holiday Cactus

  • You’ve probably seen one without knowing exactly what it was.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By the time the garden has mostly called it a year, the Thanksgiving cactus is just getting started. Its red, lavender, or soft salmon flowers appear at the tips of flat green stems, often right around the holiday, and its stems arch over the rim of the pot.

You’ve probably seen one without knowing exactly what it was. Thanksgiving and Christmas cacti often share a shelf and a label (“holiday cactus”), and both can flower in December. The giveaway is in the stems: the Thanksgiving cactus has little pointed teeth along the edges. And it’s far from the kind of cactus you’d put on your sunniest windowsill. It comes from the forests of Brazil, where it grows on trees in filtered light. Here’s what to know about the Thanksgiving cactus.

The Thanksgiving cactus (Schlumbergera truncata) is a flowering cactus native to the forests of Brazil, where it grows on trees instead of in soil. The flowers, which come in shades including white, red, lavender, and salmon-orange, typically open from mid-November through late December.

It has been revealed that look at one of the flat stem segments. On a Thanksgiving cactus, the edges have pointed teeth; on a true Christmas cactus (Schlumbergera × buckleyi), they’re rounded, like the edge of a scalloped plate.

In a recent development, set it near an east-facing window or somewhere else with bright, indirect light. When the top inch of potting mix feels dry, water it thoroughly and let the excess drain. If you’ve tucked the nursery pot into a ceramic planter, lift it out to water so it doesn’t end up sitting in a puddle.

While the plant is budding and flowering, keep the mix lightly moist. You can water less often once the flowers fade. There’s no need to repot it as soon as you bring it home; if it’s outgrown its container, wait until spring and go up one pot size.

Industry observers note that in early fall, give the plant about 14 hours of uninterrupted darkness each night for roughly six weeks. A spare room that gets daylight but where nobody switches on a lamp at night works well. Cool nights—around 55 to 60 degrees Fahrenheit—also encourage buds to form. Once you see buds, keep the plant away from drafts and don’t let the potting mix dry out completely.

Pictured above: A living room area designed by Kristen Thomas of Ink & Canvas Design.

A fresh coat of paint is one of the easiest ways to give your home a little refresh before the holidays, but you don't necessarily have to take on an entire redesign project to make an impact.

Some of the most interesting places to introduce color are the details you might normally overlook. They're relatively small surfaces, but a little paint can make them feel like intentional design features, adding character and definition without the time, expense, or commitment of repainting every wall.

Whether you want to make a statement, add a little contrast, or create a more interesting backdrop, there are plenty of ways to make a substantial visual impact with a relatively small project. Ahead, designers share the unexpected spots worth painting before the holidays and how to choose colors that feel right at home.

Window casings are an easy detail to overlook, especially when they're painted the same white as the walls and trim throughout the house. But introducing a little color around the windows “can emphasize the proportions of a window and give the room more definition,” says designer Sarah Cole. Even if you're not ready to go bold, she adds that “a subtle contrast can make a difference.”.

For a more traditional look, Kristen Thomas of Ink & Canvas Design recommends pulling from a historical or traditional palette, pointing out that “colored trim was once a sign of status in early American homes” because rich pigments were costly and difficult to come by.

According to recent reports, when time is tight before the holidays, this simple painting project can be achieved in a single afternoon. Just don’t forget the painter’s tape.

Industry observers note that don't overlook the design impact of the interior doors in your home—a hallway lined with plain white doors can feel a little forgettable, but painting one or two in a contrasting shade can give the space a more intentional look. Paint it early enough, and you may be able to hang a wreath from it.

Sources indicate that massimo Buster Minale, founder and creative director of Buster + Punch, believes an accent like this “can completely shift the character of a room.” And you don't necessarily need to choose a bright or dramatic color to get that effect. Picking one you love, rather than going all-in on a trendy shade, is key.

“I recommend choosing a grounding color and adding some whimsy with the small touches,” says Lee Crowder, National Director of Design and Model Experience at Taylor Morrison. Before painting, take a look at the doors in adjoining rooms so you can decide whether a single standout door or a more consistent color story makes the most sense.

It has been revealed that if you have built-in bookshelves or cabinetry, you already have a natural spot for a little color. Rather than repainting the entire unit, try painting just the back panels. This also gives you the opportunity to declutter what’s already there. Cole recommends this pre-holiday spot because “it adds depth and helps books and collections stand out.” Her advice for choosing a shade? “Pull a color from the room's upholstery, rug or artwork.”.

Sources indicate that thomas also recommends painting built-in shelving and cabinetry as a way to create a special feature in the room. “Painting built-ins sets them apart as a special feature and creates a beautiful backdrop for your favorite objects and holiday decor,” she notes.

Instead of going for a bold contrasting hue, Vivian Robins at Arketa Design Studio suggests using a color that already appears elsewhere in the space, explaining that this small paint revision can work as a “punctuation mark” in the room.

“Sometimes the smallest design changes create the biggest impression within a room because you're drawing out a color that lives in the space,” Robins adds.

Which Video Game Consoles Are Worth Buying in 2026?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1292 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Esquire

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the video game industry is in a wild place.
  • Sources indicate that that’s what I’m here to do, to help you weighs the pros and cons of these (mostly) years old consoles against the current price.
  • In a recent development, the PlayStation 5 is your best entryway into 4K gaming and is the best way to play GTA VI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the video game industry is in a wild place. The biggest games of the generation are coming out, Grand Theft Auto 6 on Xbox and PlayStation, and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake on Switch 2. At the same time, hardware has never been more expensive. The cheapest new consoles now start at $500, $600 if you want a PS5 (the most popular place to play GTA), with many going for more than that. To top it off with a cherry, Nintendo just hiked the price of its family friendly Switch 2 up to $500, not 18 months after its initial release. So the question now is: if you’re buying a new console in 2026, which ones are actually worth the cost?

Sources indicate that that’s what I’m here to do, to help you weighs the pros and cons of these (mostly) years old consoles against the current price. I personally love my PS5 Pro, but given the current asking price and availability, I would recommend the other, less pricey PS5 models instead to 95 percent of players. If you asked me, two years ago, if you should buy an Xbox Series S or Series S, I’d have a different answer than I do today. And then, there’s handhelds. Do you get a Switch 2 or opt for a beefier PC handheld? I’ll help you figure all that out and more, starting with the PlayStation.

In a recent development, the PlayStation 5 is your best entryway into 4K gaming and is the best way to play GTA VI. Sony has pulled ahead of Microsoft in terms of exclusive titles with games like Astro Bot, God of War: Ragnarok, and Horizon Forbidden West (and you get access to that amazing PS4 library as well). In terms of tech, the DualSense controller is an impressive leap forward when games take advantage of what it can do. The console technically supports outputs of up to 8K resolution and 120 frames per second on compatible titles. For the most part, though, you'll be playing closer to 4K60—or 4K30 in the case of GTA VI.

I've stated it before, and I'll say it again: The PS5 Disc Edition is the best console for most gamers. If you want to play GTA 6 at launch, this is probably what you should get. This edition has a disc drive, so you can pop in physical game discs or watch 4K Blu-rays. Totally worth the $650 asking price, in my opinion.

According to recent reports, if all you’re going to ever play is GTA 6 and never buy a game again, well, you can save yourself a little money and opt for the Digital Edition instead. Even the physical version of the game is just a download code in a box. The Digital Edition comes with a reduced price tag and slightly reduced bulk. No extra space for that disc drive makes it the best-looking PS5 to date. Aside from that, it's virtually identical to the regular PS5 Slim in terms of power and performance.

The PS5 Pro is mid-generation upgrade for the gamers who really care, but with things the way they are now, the enhancements are not worth it. Pre-owned Pro consoles are going from between $1,400 and $1,900 at various big box retailers, and you can’t even find new ones most days.

Certain titles like Final Fantasy VII Rebirth perform noticeably better on the Pro, and most games get some kind of boost, but it’s certainly not worth double or triple the price of what you’d otherwise be paying. The kicker is that GTA VI doesn’t even have a higher framerate mode on the Pro—it still runs at 30fps, just with fewer dips during chaotic moments as compared to the regular PS5. Even if I wanted to tell you to buy one to play the best version of GTA, I couldn’t.

In a recent development, on the Microsoft side, the Xbox Series X is the top of the line. This is where I blew through such technical powerhouses as Alan Wake 2 and Senua's Saga: Hellblade 2—two of the best-looking games I've ever played. The problem in 2026 is that, power-wise, the Series X is much closer to a regular PS5 than a PS5 Pro. And, right now, they start at $800. At that point, I’m sorry, there’s no reason not to go PlayStation.

If you're looking to play GTA 6 on an Xbox this year, I recommend the Xbox Series S instead. It launched simultaneous to the Series X as the budget alternative and, well, it still is... comparatively. The Series S is smaller, less expensive and sacrifices a disc drive. Unlike with Sony's Digital Edition PS5, there are significant tech differences between these two Xbox Series models. Most notably, it's a native 1440p console. It can upscale games to run at 4K on a 4K TV, but it can't run them natively like the Series X can. Compared to other consoles, GTA runs just as smoothly, with just as much detail thanks to Xbox’s upscaling tech, only at 1080p resolution instead of 4K. It’s another good recommendation for the casual gamer who wants to get a no-frills GTA machine as cheap as possible.

Even with a newly introduced Nintendo console coming this year, we can't ignore gaming's most popular option. Revolutionary at the time, this console combined Nintendo's console ambition with the mass appeal of its handhelds in a machine that did both. The Nintendo Switch is still affordable and family friendly, and it's the only place you can legally play Mario games. Exclusive titles like Donkey Kong: Bonanza and the Ocarina of Time remake bolster the existing library and give a reason to upgrade.

Recent findings suggest that still, I have a hard time recommending any gamer still happy with their Switch upgrade for the sake of it. The leap just isn’t that monumental. That being said I won’t hesitate to recommend the Switch 2 for anyone upcoming to the hardware. It’s objectively better and the longevity will be worth the price difference.

Industry observers note that GTA 6 might not be coming to PC right away, but that isn't a good reason to neglect my personal handheld of choice. Ever since the introduction of the Steam Deck, the PC-gaming market has been going increasingly mobile. And the upgraded OLED model is still the gold standard—trust me, I’ve tried them all.

In a recent development, my top recommendation for the average console gamer is the Steam Deck OLED. It runs on Valve's SteamOS, so you don't even have to worry about learning Windows (like some kind of PC gamer). The Steam Deck UI completely console-ifies your entire Steam library and makes it easy for newbies to jump in. If you're used to the Switch, you may find it to be a bit beefy, but once I got used to it, I actually found the Steam Deck OLED to be the most ergonomic of all PC-gaming handhelds.

Sources indicate that it's never been a better time to get your feet wet, buy some games on Steam (wait for a sale; there will be plenty), and see what all the fuss is about. If the price looks prohibitive and you don't care much about graphics, get the cheaper LCD model while it's still being sold.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you shop as much as ELLE’s beauty-obsessed editors, you’re already pretty familiar with a few common skin care ingredients. Those with acne-prone skin know the benefits of salicylic acid, retinol, and mandelic acid all too well. Oily skin types typically reach for non-comedogenic formulas, while dry skin drinks up hyaluronic acid. Still, if there’s one ingredient all skin types can use in a routine, it’s ceramides. Newly introduced to that world? Let us help you get more familiar.

“Ceramides are fats, or lipids, that your skin makes on its own,” explains Dr. Anne Han. While you might not have heard of them, think of ceramides as your skin’s security guard. “They make up about half of the lipids in the stratum corneum, the outermost layer of skin. I like the ‘brick and mortar’ picture: skin cells are the bricks, and ceramides, along with cholesterol and fatty acids, are the mortar that holds them together. That mortar keeps water in and keeps irritants, allergens, and microbes out,” she adds. When your skin becomes particularly dry and crackly, this could be a sign that it needs a ceramide boost.

It has been revealed that “When ceramide levels drop, the barrier gets ‘leaky.’ Water evaporates more easily, and skin turns dry, tight, flaky, itchy, and more reactive. That happens with eczema, as we age, in cold, dry weather, and with overwashing or harsh actives. Ceramides in a moisturizer help top up what the skin is missing,” Dr. Han shares. Not all skin care products offer instant gratification, but adding a ceramide moisturizer to your lineup can boost moisture levels “sometimes within a day of the first use, with more benefit after a few weeks of steady use,” Dr. Han suggests, adding that “studies show ceramide moisturizers raise skin hydration and cut water loss” and “work best alongside cholesterol and fatty acids, the other two parts of the skin’s natural lipid mix, not on their own.”.

All in all, every skin type can benefit from a ceramide moisturizer for an instant boost of moisture and overall improvement in skin over time. If your skin is in need of a tune-up, the list below, featuring derm- and ELLE editor-approved picks, is the perfect place to start. Shop every type of formula, from K-beauty staples to splurge-worthy finds.

It has been revealed that this fan-favorite CeraVe cream has reached cult status for good reason. As with most formulas from the brand, this moisturizing tub is packed with ceramides and hyaluronic acid, which lock in and attract moisture, respectively.

Key ingredients: Hyaluronic acid, ceramides.

Expert review: “[This has] several skin-identical ceramides with glycerin, is fragrance-free, works for face and body, and is affordable.”—Dr. Anne Han, MD.

Recent findings suggest that the powerhouse trio in this formula plays key roles in restoring and balancing the skin: ceramides protect, niacinamide addresses discoloration, and glycerin provides moisture. Together, they leave your skin deeply nourished and supple. Take it a step further with the SPF 30 version for even more protection.

Key ingredients: Prebiotic thermal water, ceramides, niacinamide, glycerin.

Industry observers note that expert review: “It contains ceramides plus niacinamide, which can calm redness.”—Dr. Han.

While a hydrated, moisturized barrier can improve the look of fine lines and wrinkles, this SkinCeuticals formula is designed to deliver a healthy moisture boost. With vitamin E, lipids, essential oils, and more, skin becomes smoother, suppler, and plumper with every use.

Key ingredients: Ceramides, vitamin E, essential oils.

Expert review: “This has the full barrier-lipid trio, which is helpful for aging skin that recovers more slowly.”—AH.

Packed with everything we love about K-beauty formulas—lightweight, hydrating, soothing—this barrier cream seeps into the skin like butter, improving its elasticity and suppleness.

Key ingredients: Ceramides, fatty acids, and cholesterol.

Recent findings suggest that ELLE editor review: “Believe it or not, my foray into Korean skin care came through Aestura’s products. In the dead of winter, when my semi-oily, acne-prone skin needed reprieve, I received a gift set with the brand’s bestsellers and instantly fell for this cream. My skin felt so hydrated and conditioned, and it even helped my makeup look more glowy (not greasy).”—Nerisha Penrose, beauty commerce editor.

It has been revealed that you’ve likely seen a TikTok video of someone applying this milky solution to their skin during a skin care routine or makeup tutorial. The barrier-strengthening “glazing milk” gives you an instant glow while working overtime to soothe and quench parched skin.

Key ingredients: Ceramide, vitamin E.

Customer review: “Oh how I love this essence. I usually use a thinner/clear essence but I am now a fan of this milky one. It gives an instant boost of hydration and helps with serum absorption.”.

Recent findings suggest that medik8’s formulas are as straightforward as they come, with ceramides showing up in this moisturizer and its nighttime counterpart. In this composition, the main ingredient is combined with hyaluronic acid and peptides to protect stressed skin and visibly plump stressed skin over time.

Key ingredients: Ceramides, prebiotic peptides, hyaluronic acid.

In a recent development, customer review: “My skin feels great when I use it. Light enough for my oily skin but truly moisturizing, unlike others I’ve tried over the years which were either too light or too heavy.”.

In a recent development, as the name suggests, the results are, in fact, instant. Think of this moisturizer as youthfulness in a bottle; it’s packed with moisturizing glycerin and urea, plus squalane, peptides, and ceramides for firming.

Key ingredients: Peptide blend (Dipalmityl hydroxylproline and hexapeptide-12), squalane, ceramides, glycerin, urea, and hyaluronic acid.

Recent findings suggest that ELLE editor review: “Look into my travel toiletry bag, and you’ll find about two of these tubes rolled down to their last squeeze—that’s just how much I love this cream. My skin feels instantly moisturized and supple, but looks even better when I wake up.”—NP.

There’s power in numbers, so when shopping for an effective ceramide moisturizer, Dr. Han advises looking for one that combines similar ingredients. “Look for ceramides together with cholesterol and fatty acids, which mimic the skin’s own lipid mix. Ceramides used alone are less effective at barrier repair,” she says. Plus, look for formulas with “skin-identical” ceramides, which look like “ceramide NP, AP, or EOP (older names include ceramide 1, 3, and 6-II)” on labels.

In a recent development, furthermore, you’ll want a moisturizer packed with “humectants, like glycerin or hyaluronic acid [which] pull water in” or “occlusives, like petrolatum or dimethicone to seal [moisture] in; niacinamide can help skin make more ofits own ceramides,” Dr. Han adds. Other important markers to look for include “fragrance-free” to avoid irritating sensitive or eczema-prone skin; for acne-prone skin, “non-comedogenic” products are great because they don’t clog pores.

“They do different jobs, so it isn’t really either/or. Ceramides are barrier ingredients and help the skin hold water and resist irritation, and that is what makes something a moisturizer,” Dr. Han explains. Meanwhile, peptides—skin care’s buzziest ingredient—are touted for their anti-aging properties. “They are meant to signal the skin to make more collagen or to soften the look of fine lines. If your main concern is dryness, sensitivity, redness, or eczema-prone skin, start with ceramides. The science behind them is more direct, since you are replacing a lipid your barrier actually lacks. If your barrier is in good shape and you want something for fine lines, a peptide product is a reasonable, gentle add-on,” she adds.

Above: Inside Carolina Herrera’s Miami flagship, a sculptural chandelier by artist Liz Oliver hangs suspended above a soft pink couch.

In September, Carolina Herrera held an extravaganza of a runway show during New York Fashion Week, celebrating the brand’s 45th anniversary. This past week, the festivities went further south, to Miami. Last Thursday night, creative director Wes Gordon and members of the city’s fashion and arts community gathered beneath a cherry-red awning to toast the brand’s newest boutique—and sixth official location in the U.S.

Opened on August 15, the 3,000-square-foot shop sits in the middle of the Miami Design District, with a dramatic arched entrance welcoming guests into the limestone-finished structure. Designed in collaboration with interior designers Brandi Howe and Jessica Hyland of Hyland Studio, the store is bursting with color and feminine details—soft pink travertine covers the floor while furnishings feature red and pink accents. In the center of the main salon, a custom pink sofa with graceful curvature offers an elegant seat; in another area, the same red awning from the boutique’s entrance reappears suspended over a pair of regal armchairs.

“The Carolina Herrera woman is bold, elegant, and joyful. She embraces color, expresses herself with confidence, and never shies away from making an entrance,” claims Gordon.

But the fresh store is not only an ode to the Carolina Herrera brand but also to other female creatives. On view throughout the space are artworks commissioned specifically for the boutique as a part of the Carolina Herrera for Women in the Arts initiative. In the main salon, Los Angeles-based artist Liz Oliver designed a rose-colored textile installation that doubles as a sculptural chandelier. Elsewhere, ceramic planters made by the women-owned Choplet Ceramics are on display. Throughout the boutique, a recurring custom floral motif by Argentine artist Constanza Vallese appears on vases and tables.

According to recent reports, in raising a glass to the boutique, guests at last Thursday’s event honored both the Carolina Herrera woman and her new city. “Her energy is magnetic—much like the spirit of Miami,” says Gordon. “It feels entirely natural that we should open our next home here.”.

7 Home Organizing Trends That Will Be EVERYWHERE in 2027, According to Pros

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Although trends prevail in the interior design world, they also can find their way into other areas beyond decor—such as home organization.
  • As we look to the year ahead, four professional organizers are here to share what they think will be the top organizing trends.
  • While AI has been all over the place, from work to our personal lives—it appears to be tapering off, according to Lenora O’Keith, decluttering and organizing expert and owner of Aronel Home.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Although trends prevail in the interior design world, they also can find their way into other areas beyond decor—such as home organization. Creating orderly spaces can make life a lot easier. While tried-and-true solutions are still around, there are always fresh ways to tackle organizing projects.

As we look to the year ahead, four professional organizers are here to share what they think will be the top organizing trends.

While AI has been all over the place, from work to our personal lives—it appears to be tapering off, according to Lenora O’Keith, decluttering and organizing expert and owner of Aronel Home.

In a recent development, “AI and smart home solutions were everywhere at the beginning of the year, but there’s definitely been a lot of AI fatigue and a push for ‘dumb tech’ lately,” she shares. “When working with clients, a lot of them are over AI being added into everything. They just want simple solutions that work.” This can include things like setting up a household command center and labeling storage containers.

According to recent reports, moving has traditionally been a stressful experience that you were expected to figure out on your own—but that may be changing. Allison Flinn, owner of Reclaim Professional Organizing, says that more people are taking advantage of organizing services when they move.

“You can pack and unpack, but you won't truly have a fully functional and an organized fresh home if you haven't decluttered prior to moving or aren't intentional during the unpacking process by implementing a system that truly works for your lifestyle,” she says.

Instead of doing what a lot of us do—devising storage systems for each individual space—2027 may welcome the idea that you should treat your home as an entire unit to be organized.

Michelle Urban, owner and founder of The Organized House, says that people are increasingly not treating each room as its own one-off organizing project. She says that instead, they’re looking at how belongings move from one space to another and where they need to be throughout the day. For instance, items like backpacks, shoes, and sports gear may land in the entry, get stored in the garage, and need to be back by the door the next morning.

“When those spaces are planned together, the system supports the family’s routine instead of just moving things from one pile to another,” Urban indicates.

Sources indicate that viewed more holistically, experts are also seeing that organizing isn’t just an occasional task, but something to stay on top of each week. “I think more homeowners will begin to view organization as ongoing home maintenance rather than a one-time project,” says Ashley Bailey, founder and professional organizer at Everything Orderly. “Just like other aspects of maintaining a home, organizing requires occasional attention as our lives and needs change.”.

In a recent development, flinn claims that more and more people are outsourcing household tasks to a home manager or home concierge. In addition to handling things like doing laundry, returning packages, and making doctor’s appointments, these professionals can also help you organize your home in just a few hours a week.

Eco-friendly everything is still as popular as ever, and it even applies to how we organize our homes. While O’Keith claims that sustainability never really goes out of style, homeowners are increasingly turning to eco-friendly organizing products—specifically, by avoiding plastic and embracing natural materials like bamboo, rattan, and sea grass for baskets and bins.

Sources indicate that but she says that there is a exception for basements and attics. “I always recommend heavy-duty plastic storage [for these areas],” O’Keith says. “Since those spaces deal with dampness, temperature changes, and pests, other materials could get damaged easily.”.

While it can be lovely to live in a well-designed, beautiful home, if there isn’t function, you might make your daily life more difficult. That’s why people are going beyond Instagram-ready interiors and are wrapping in plenty of function.

Urban believes that progressively more people are bringing functional storage into a room’s design, and it isn’t just an add-on.

“A credenza can hold games in the living room; a dining room buffet can store wrapping paper and party decor between celebrations,” Urban points out. “As rooms take on more jobs, people want storage that looks like it belongs and does a useful job.”.

As we head into 2027, people are thinking about their budgets more and more, which is why using items you already have as storage solutions is cost-effective.

According to recent reports, “I'm seeing more clients interested in making better use of what they already own rather than automatically purchasing newly introduced organizing products,” Bailey says. For instance, she recently took on a project that transformed a playroom, but used items the family already had.

In a recent development, “Sometimes the best solution isn't another organizing product. It's rethinking how you're using the space and what you already have,” she says. “I think we'll see more emphasis on thoughtful editing and repurposing before purchasing something new.”.

If Esquire’s list of the greatest sports movies of all time was accompanied by a training montage, it’d look something like this: the entertainment editors hunkered down at home, night after night, watching (and rewatching) our way through the great canon of this beloved genre. Caddyshack, still a blast. Talladega Nights, again? Twist my arm. A first watch of Breaking Away, a blind spot no more. Remember the Titans, for probably the seventeenth time.

Smash cut to us fighting about which films were truly worthy of our final top fifty. A long debate about whether or not The Color of Money is actually better than The Hustler. An editor’s brilliant suggestion that The Fast & the Furious: Tokyo Drift is actually a sports movie. A mutual decision to cut Friday Night Lights because, really, does it deserve to be here if the TV show is the one we remember most?

Final shot: the writing. Writing. Writing. Writing.

Now, this is the part where you take it all in, rewatch one (or four) of your favorites, decide what you agree with, what you simply cannot stand for, and let us know about it. Let’s walk through the tunnel together, shall we? These are the best fifty sports movies of all time.—Brady Langmann.

In a recent development, burt Reynolds stars in The Longest Yard as the incarcerated former quarterback, Paul "Wrecking" Crewe, who was kicked out of the NFL after admitting to point shaving. While in prison, he convinces the football-obsessed warden to let the inmates play a game of football against the guards, even though the seemingly harmless activity only exacerbates the power dynamic between them. But unlike most underdog sports stories, The Longest Yard’s setting pushes themes of reclaiming your self-worth in the face of a cruel, authoritarian system much more than its competition. —Josh Rosenberg.

The Pride of the Yankees arguably did more for the legacy of its star, Gary Cooper, than its subject, baseball legend Lou Gehrig, but it was 1942 for goodness’ sake. The film was rushed into production and premiered in theaters just a little over a year after the Fresh York Yankees player died from a rare disease that would later be named after him. And if it wasn’t for Cooper’s incredibly earnest portrayal, the conventional biopic likely wouldn’t have had the same effect—even with recency bias and Babe Ruth playing himself. But twenty bucks indicates you can’t watch Cooper give Gehrig’s real-life farewell speech at the end of the film without shedding a tear. —J.R.

The first time the Fast & Furious franchise swerved from street races and highway heists came in the standalone 2006 sequel, Tokyo Drift—the first helmed by Fast Saga mainstay Justin Lin. Set in the world of Japanese drift racing (originated by motorcyclist Kunimitsu Takahashi and mastered by “Drift King” Keiichi Tsuchiya), troubled American teenager Sean (Lucas Black) moves to Japan to live with his father, where he gets caught up in the motorsport’s resurgent scene. Basically The Karate Kid on wheels, The Fast & the Furious: Tokyo Drift is about the only time these movies proved it didn’t need Vin Diesel and barbecues to be a thrill. —Eric Francisco.

We know what you’re thinking: Clint Eastwood’s Million Dollar Baby exists. But allow us to make a case for his 2009 drama Invictus. Set in 1995, after apartheid, Invictus reveals how the Springboks national rugby team—led by Francois Pienaar, played by Matt Damon—united South Africa through their victory (spoilers?) at the 1995 Rugby World Cup. One of their biggest motivators was Nelson Mandela (Morgan Freeman), whose democratically elected presidency was equally symbolic of South Africa’s journey to reconciliation. Where Million Dollar Baby was a deeply personal (and harrowing) tale of one woman in the boxing ring, Invictus is about an entire nation in desperate need of something to believe in. —E.F.

Recent findings suggest that the Big Lebowski is a bowling movie. You might not think about that right away, especially since the Joel and Ethan Coen comedy starring Jeff Bridges starts with a California slacker who’s simply on the search for his missing rug. But amid all the crime capers and accidental kidnapping plots, the heart of The Big Lebowski is a film about a group of guys—including John Goodman and Steve Buscemi, a.k.a. the dream blunt-rotation bowling team—who just want to take down rival bowler Jesus Quintana (John Turturro). If Hollywood ever makes a traditional bowling movie as good as The Big Lebowski, you can bet that it will still be compared to The Dude every step of the way. —J.R.

How many sports movies actually created a team? Only The Mighty Ducks. In the original that started it all, Emilio Estevez stars as a hotshot lawyer whose community service leads him to coach a ragtag youth hockey team. During his state-mandated service, he rediscovers his lost love for the ice. There have been sequels and even a two-season Disney+ revival series—and Disney’s brief ownership of a real franchise, the Anaheim Ducks, who won the Stanley Cup in 2007—but the first movie is still undefeated. Ducks Never Say Die! —E.F.

Industry observers note that in 2011, the MMA business was booming. Tickets were through the roof, the UFC was finding its place on primetime, and new leagues like ONE Championship took off. So it was a good time for Gavin O’Connor to unleash his smashing drama, Warrior. Tom Hardy and Joel Edgerton play two estranged brothers whose entry in a mixed martial arts tournament forces them to confront their fractured relationship. Warrior hits hardest where it counts, and functions as an early showcase of Tom Hardy’s brawny charisma. —E.F.

According to recent reports, I’m not one of those sickos who wishes that rollerball was a real sport, but that doesn’t mean I don’t enjoy watching it. Especially when, in the dystopian world of the fictitious sport—which combines roller derby, handball, biking, and outright bloodthirst—James Caan is the GOAT. The ‘70s cult classic earns its spot in our rankings not because of the rollerball action (which is thrillingly directed by Norman Jewison), or its retro-futuristic set design, but because of its prescient vision of a sports league that is shrouded in rich, manipulative C-suiters and a controlling body that, well, only wants to control. —B.L.

Industry observers note that nobody respects the referee. And why should they? They’re always slowing down the game and making terrible calls. I mean, are they blind, dumb, or both, you know what I’m saying? Well, when fanatical baseball fan (and umpire hater) Bill Johnson (William Bendix) is forced to go to umpire school after losing his job in this silly 1950s comedy, we all learn a thing or two about why the game actually needs an impartial bystander who keeps the game clean. Even if he can’t seem to see the damn ball. —J.R.

It has been revealed that is the John Huston movie where Sylvester Stallone and Michael Caine play POWs at a German camp who form a soccer team, play said Nazis in soccer, and escape at the end of the game extremely cheesy? Yes, it absolutely is. But is it ... also sort of amazing to watch Stallone earnestly play goalie, Caine direct his squad like a seasoned Premier League manager, and Pelé—yes, Pelé is in this film—deke up some Bambi-legged Nazis? Also yes. I won’t spoil the method in which Pelé scores a goal, but it’s so stupidly fun that it solidified Victory’s place on this list. —B.L.

Sources indicate that want a sports-movie take that has earned me some flak around the Esquire office? Of the two Ron Shelton-directed, Kevin Costner-starring sports movies—Tin Cup and Bull Durham, of course—I much prefer Tin Cup. The golf comedy has it all: a perfectly sleazy Costner performance, the sly intellectualism of Bull Durham, a pitch-perfect Tex-Mex backdrop, a Cheech Marin-played caddy, and, most importantly, a Jim Nantz cameo. Its premise, which sees a problematic ex-pro take another shot at the PGA Tour, has more influence than you’d think; look no further than Owen Wilson’s Apple TV comedy Stick, which plays like a loving homage to Tin Cup, right down to the shaggy Winnebago. —B.L.

Industry observers note that dodgeball is, without question, one of the stupidest movies ever made. Even among the Anchormans and American Pies of the late nineties/early 2000s, this sports comedy starring Vince Vaughn and Ben Stiller about a group of average Joes who compete in a dodgeball tournament to save their gym from being taken over by a fat-shaming, corporate fitness giant has no business being packed to the gills with so many memorably hilarious lines. I wish we had a hundred more movies where Stiller is the antagonist, because his fitness freak White Goodman is one of the funniest villains of all time. Dodgeball even inspired ESPN to actually air bizarre sports on its fictional spinoff channel ESPN 8 “The Ocho,” and I can’t say any other sports comedies ever had that much of an impact on the real world. —J.R.

Recent findings suggest that when I saw The Way Back, which stars Ben Affleck as a struggling alcoholic who is asked to return to his high school to coach its basketball team, I immediately felt like it was one of the greatest sports movies ever made. That was at a press screening in March 2020—you can see where I’m going with this. The pandemic washed out what should’ve been a genuine moment for Affleck and the film, because The Way Back is a stunning character portrait with one of the boldest endings in all of sports cinema. I noted this to its writer, Task creator Brad Ingelsby, around this time last year. “I think it's one of the best performances Ben's ever given,” Ingelsby told me. “I really believe that.” That makes two of us. —B.L.

In a recent development, breaking Away might just be the most underappreciated film on this list. How underappreciated? Well, all three of us hadn’t seen it until longtime Esquire research editor Kevin McDonnell alerted us to its greatness. And damn, was he right. On the surface, Breaking Away is a classic midwestern coming-of-age dramedy: Four teenagers (played by Dennis Christopher, Dennis Quaid, Daniel Stern, and Jackie Earle Haley) clumsily figure out post-high-school life amidst the class wars of Bloomington, Indiana. But Breaking Away’s Oscar-winning screenplay—which layers a climactic cycling competition on top of it all—is so damn smart, funny, and full of teenage heartache that you’ll wish Hollywood made more like it nowadays. Or, at the very least, more high-stakes biking movies. —B.L.

According to recent reports, after The Wolf of Wall Street and Suicide Squad, Margot Robbie became Hollywood’s new it girl. But her Oscar-nominated performance as controversial skater Tonya Harding in the 2017 crime biopic I, Tonya, cemented her prestige status. The movie is based on the life of Harding, her contentious relationship with her mother (played by Allison Janney), and her connections to the infamous 1994 assault on rival Nancy Kerrigan. Robbie pulls out all the stops for a 10/10/10 performance, with an extreme focus on ice skating as a tougher, dirtier sport than the bedazzled outfits imply. —E.F.

Cool Runnings isn’t just a joke. As funny as a Jamaican bobsleigh team is—and was when the real-life team debuted at the 1988 Winter Olympics—Canadian actor John Candy (Planes, Trains and Automobiles) wouldn’t star in a comedy film in the nineties coaching a ridiculous sports team unless it also had some heart. Luckily, Cool Runnings has loads of it. The good-natured comedy for the whole family was a smash crowd pleaser. It took the focus off the Olympics’ superhuman competitors and proved that anything was attainable with the right camaraderie. —J.R.

It has been revealed that mention the Von Erichs to anyone of a certain age from Texas, and they’ll tell you how crucial they were to the community—and how cursed they might have all been. Based on true events, Sean Durkin’s musclebound tragedy follows the rise and demise of the Texas wrestling dynasty, the Von Erichs. As the owners and stars of World Class Championship Wrestling, the Von Erichs were on their way to immortality until a series of events tore them apart. Though The Iron Claw is packed with body slams and sweat, its story about the strength of brotherhood in the face of tyrannical masculinity makes it a transcendent tear-jerker. —E.F.

Recent findings suggest that it’s to be expected for sports movies to be about dirty, dehydrated athletes. But only Bring It On dared to fix its cameras on the cheerleaders. An early 2000s classic and a cable TV staple, the movie follows the rivalry between an affluent suburban cheerleading team (led by Kirsten Dunst) and an inner-city Los Angeles squad (led by Gabrielle Union). After Dunst’s character learns her team’s dynamite routine was stolen from the East Compton Clovers, she works to come up with a new idea from scratch before a national competition. Don’t let the high-pitched cheers and pearly white teeth fool you; Bring It On is an honest-to-goodness examination of cultural appropriation and the class and cultural divisions even amongst American youth. —E.F.

It has been revealed that timothée Chalamet, who has a debilitating fear of heights, stood atop the Las Vegas Sphere to promote Marty Supreme. While the man went home from the Oscars without a statue, he still left behind one of the best, unlikeliest sports movies in recent memory. Set in 1952, Marty Supreme stars Chalamet as an ambitious hustler with a silver tongue (and orange balls) who is dead set on serving as America’s emissary in the most exciting sport of the postwar era: ping pong. Essentially Uncut Gems in pleated pants, Marty Supreme isn’t actually about table tennis, but about the hustle, and whether it’s in your favor or not, you have to respect it. —E.F.

I’m a sucker for Rounders. The 1998 indie gem starring a cooler-than-all-of-us Matt Damon and a peaking Ed Norton as poker sharks is still a brilliant watch. And I’d be remiss if I didn’t mention the ace up Rounders’s sleeve: A terrifying villain in John Malkovich’s Teddy KGB (the name still gets me), who you genuinely believe would drain the life savings of a guy like Damon’s Mike McDermott and not give a single shit about it. Give Rounders a watch today, and it’s hard not to feel how visionary it was in showing how young men’s lives are hooked, warped, and ruined by the allure of gambling. Remake Rounders today and McDermott might just have DraftKings and FanDuel as the most-used apps on his phone. —B.L.

The Karate Kid is one of the main reasons why I took up martial arts as a child (along with Power Rangers), and I imagine it was much the same for most nineties kids. Not just because Daniel LaRusso (Ralph Macchio) and Rocky director John G. Avildsen replicated Stallone’s underdog magic for teenagers, but because the film helped create one of the best spiritual mentors of all time in the late Pat Morita’s Mr. Miyagi. There are few training methods as iconic as “wax on, wax off” and few villainous looks more menacing than “sweep the leg, Johnny.” But if you master the former, and avoid the latter, you just might learn what martial arts are really about. —J.R.

According to recent reports, how Warner Bros. ever convinced basketball phenom Michael Jordan to star in this half-animated/half-live-action Looney Tunes basketball movie is beyond me. Because, if I’m Michael Jordan, you show me any storyboard frame from this film during pre-production and I’m bolting for the door faster than the Road Runner. But I’m beyond grateful that the basketball GOAT saw the vision behind Space Jam, because it’s unbelievable how this film wasn’t just an achievement in animation but also one of the greatest sports movies of all time. Really think about that for a second. One of the most celebrated, family-friendly sports movies of all time stars Michael Jordan and Bugs Bunny. Who could have seen that coming? —J.R.

Kumite! Kumite! Kumite! The movie that cemented Jean-Claude Van Damme’s status as the coolest ass-kicker of the 1980s, Bloodsport is still a good time even if it can’t shed its beefcake cheese. It is based on the very tall tales (read: bullshit) of Frank Dux, who claimed to be a U.S. Marine and ninjutsu master who won a secret underground tournament in Hong Kong. Whatever. Bloodsport still rocks as an exhibition of JCVD at his prime. It is The Karate Kid for dudes cracking open mini-fridge beers, and it’s awesome. Fun fact: The original Mortal Kombat started out as a pitch for a Van Damme arcade game due to the success of Bloodsport. —E.F.

There are plenty of movies like Slap Shot in the sports-movie oeuvre: a great athlete, nearing the end of his time in the game, undergoes an existential crisis that somehow turns into one last great winning run. It’s just that Paul Newman did it best in Slap Shot. The 1977 comedy, which follows a mess of a hockey team that turns to outright violence to win games and boost fan interest (however morbid) is still an absolute blast to watch, especially when those damn Hanson brothers drop their gloves. Heated Rivalry could never! —B.L.

Sources indicate that the WNBA was in its infancy when Gina Prince-Bythewood’s Love & Basketball hit the court. Sanaa Lathan stars as Monica, a girl with hoop dreams who grows up next door to Quincy (Omar Epps), the son of an NBA baller. As they grow up as childhood best friends before becoming lovers in college, Monica and Quincy eventually learn to square their relationship with their professional aspirations. In most sports movies, romance is a subplot for the main character. Here, love is the very name of the game. And it’s a slam dunk. —E.F.

You can think of Major League as a funnier, better Ted Lasso set in the world of professional baseball (and the Hannah Waddingham analogue an actual villain). Tom Berenger, Charlie Sheen, Wesley Snipes, and more fill out the roster of the Cleveland Indians. After a vindictive newly introduced owner (Margaret Whitton) buys the team and prepares a move to Miami, the players spend their final season dramatically improving their game just out of spite. Everything comes down to a climactic division playoff game against the one and only New York Yankees. It’s a cliché to call Major League a “home run” or whatever, so instead I’ll just say it has nice velocity. —E.F.

In my book, The Hustler is the greater billiards film over its legacy sequel, The Color of Money. (Sadly, I was overruled.) Sure, the latter has Tom Cruise. But the original black-and-white Paul Newman film better captures the stress of betting on pool, swathed in the smoke of cigars and just the right blood-alcohol level to concentrate without second-guessing yourself. Throw in George C. Scott as a professional gambler and Jackie Gleason as pool shark Minnesota Fats, and you have one of the most star-studded and high-stakes films of the sixties—all over the act of poking some billiard balls into table pockets. —J.R.

Never before has tennis been so exhilarating—and, we’ll say it, titillating. Luca Guadagnino’s meme machine of 2024, Challengers, raised the bar as an erotic sports drama about two former best friends (Josh O’Connor and Mike Faist) torn apart over a beautiful tennis ace (Zendaya). During their tense reunion at a rinky-dink tournament, they compete to settle things once and for all. Between Guadagnino’s dizzying camera and the dynamic duo of Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross going beast mode on the soundtrack, Challengers had us all spending one summer bringing our situationships to the theater. It was a weird summer, admittedly. —E.F.

Who can forget the Beast, or Wendy Peffercorn, or those long summer nights playing ball under glittering fireworks? The Sandlot is the ultimate love letter to adolescent, Americana-flavored nostalgia, where boyhood friendships are forged in the cauldron of baseball. Set in 1962 in the San Fernando Valley, new kid Smalls (Tom Guiry) joins with other neighborhood kids who occupy an empty sandlot for their own baseball games. Over a long and fateful summer, Smalls makes memories that will last a lifetime. But he’ll always be a square—the kid’s a square! —E.F.

Recent findings suggest that if the word “manifesting” could be defined by any movie, it’s Rudy. Sean Astin stars as real-life former Notre Dame Fighting Irish football player Daniel “Rudy” Ruettiger, a young man with learning disabilities whose dreams of playing football for the University of Notre Dame seem out of reach. Somehow, Rudy gets his opportunity—but only after incredible amounts of patience, perseverance, and resolve in the face of those who want to bring you down. Next to Rocky, Rudy is one of the greatest underdog sports dramas ever made, one that can inspire just about anyone to get off the couch and make their own dreams a reality. —E.F.

Chariots of Fire is the most serious capital-F film on this list. The British historical drama was nominated for seven awards at the 1982 Academy Awards, winning Best Picture, Best Screenplay, Best Costume Design, and Best Score for its portrayal of two real-life track stars, Harold Abrahams and Eric Liddell (one Jewish, the other a Scottish Christian), who overcame prejudice to compete for their country in the 1924 Olympic Games. Vangelis’s score, and the scene of the track team running on the beach in slow motion, remain Chariots’ lasting impact forty years later. But don’t let modern pastiches and parodies of the film sour the original’s legacy. Chariots of Fire is as much a fascinating picture of England in between the world wars as it is one of the most inspiring sports films of all time. —J.R.

Sources indicate that W.C. Fields once stated that his one piece of advice for show business was to “never work with children or animals.” Years later, Kelsey Grammer said a similar thing when he agreed to star in the Cheers spinoff, Frasier: “No kids, no dogs, and no wives.” But if Walter Matthau followed that rule, we would have never arrived at The Bad News Bears—a heartwarming family comedy about a beer-slugging Little League baseball coach and his ragtag group of kids who have no idea why their parents force them to play baseball over the summer. But just maybe, this oddball group of losers can help us all remember that everyone deserves to enjoy the great American game regardless of which team runs around the bases more than the other. —J.R.

In a recent development, if Talladega Nights isn’t the most quotable film of all time (“Dear 8 pounds 6 ounces newborn infant Jesus, don't even know a word yet...”) it’s at least the most quotable sports movie of all time. (One more: “Chip, I'm all jacked up on Mountain Dew!”) One of Will Ferrell and Adam McKay’s greatest collaborations during their undefeated run in the aughts, the epic NASCAR spoof—which pits drivers played by Ferrell, John C. Reilly, and Sacha Baron Cohen in a gasoline-slicked competitive love-hate triangle—is a riot twenty(!) years later. Why has Talladega Nights stood the test of time? You could say it’s all thanks to Ferrell and McKay’s sharply written, gag-stuffed script—complete with an iconic Applebee’s scene. Or even the racing scenes themselves, which are downright thrilling. (Watching Ricky and Cal pull the slingshot move still gets me.) But it’s the tour de force comedic turns by leading men Ferrell, Reilly, and Cohen that make Talladega Nights a film that’ll hold this spot for another two decades more. —B.L.

Here’s what Ford v Ferrari is about on the surface: Matt Damon plays real-life auto designer Carroll Shelby who, along with Christian Bale as English racer Ken Miles, is hired by Ford to beat the dominant Ferrari at the legendary 24 Hours of Le Mans in 1966. While Ford is in it to boost car sales, Shelby and Miles are in it to win it, to prove American muscle has what it takes to compete on the world stage. But here’s what James Mangold’s 2019 masterpiece is really about: Can art survive under commerce? Look under the hood, past the gears and the minutiae of automotive design, and what you have are artists trying to exercise brilliance under breakneck pressure. Between that and its abundance of menswear inspo, Ford v Ferrari isn’t just one of the best sports movies or racing movies—it is hands-down one of the best movies, period. —E.F.

In a recent development, there is no crying in baseball, but there’s so much more too. Primarily set during World War II, when professional baseball players served abroad, an all-women’s league begins to satisfy a baseball-starved public. The movie follows the Rockford Peaches—coached by drunk, acerbic Jimmy Dugan (Tom Hanks)—who become one of the most popular teams in the beautiful but short lifespan of the All-American Girls Professional Baseball League. Geena Davis stars as the Peaches’ best player, whose relationship with her sister (Lori Petty) serves as the movie’s main emotional engine. A wholesome ode to sisterhood, to baseball, and to knowing the good ol’ days when you’re in them, A League of Their Own is truly in a league of its own. The 2022 Prime Video revival series, which ran for a single season, is also worth checking out. —E.F.

Released just one year before Field of Dreams, Kevin Costner stars in Bull Durham as “Crash” Davis, a veteran baseball catcher brought in to coach a hotshot minor league pitching prospect (Tim Robbins) with a “million dollar arm, but a five cent head.” Unlike Field, Angels in the Outfield, or any of the God-meets-baseball sports movie canon, Bull Durham establishes right away that baseball might be like a religion, but it’s also like sex. So, as Costner works on the brash rookie in the dugout, baseball groupie Annie (Susan Sarandon) finds success taming the bull in the bedroom. “The stadiums are like cathedrals,” Costner tells the team. “The hotels all have room service, and the women all have long legs and brains.” It may not be a conventional baseball film, nor a traditional rom-com, but Bull Durham is all about the mind games that get in the way of great play. And, of course, Sarandon’s undeniable sex appeal. —J.R.

Sources indicate that happy Gilmore is a living, breathing embodiment of everything that makes Adam Sandler great. The golf comedy is packed with heart, still-funny one-liners (“The price is wrong, bitch!”), and slapstick shenanigans that only the Sandman could pull off. Add a wonderfully sincere Carl Weathers performance, a pitch-perfect cartoon-villain turn from Christopher McDonald, and a still-great Bob Barker cameo and you have a generational comedy. Plus, the golf is still so believably tense that you’ll still second-guess every one of Happy’s putts on a rewatch. And I dare you to listen to Lynyrd Skynyrd’s “Tuesday’s Gone” and not get the chills. —B.L.

According to recent reports, there’s an entire subgenre of sports films that tie religion to baseball. Hell, there’s even another film higher up on this list that may deserve the title of best baseball movie ever over The Natural. But the Robert Redford-starring film about a kid from the Midwest who is seemingly chosen by God to inspire people with baseball after lightning strikes a tree on his family farm and he carves a bat from it by hand still lives up to its mythical story. Every impossible home run that Redford’s Roy Hobbs hits in The Natural would be the greatest thing you’ve ever seen happen at a baseball game, made even more iconic by Randy Newman’s Superman (1978)-esque score. —J.R.

In a recent development, few comedies have remained as quotable as Caddyshack over the last four decades. Sure, it helps that the screwball golf film stars a murderers’ row of Chevy Chase, Rodney Dangerfield, Bill Murray, and director Harold Ramis. But even outside of the joy of Dangerfield pulling a boombox out of his golf club bag and exclaiming, “So what? So let's dance!”, or Bill Murray relentlessly playing whack-a-mole with gophers, Caddyshack is a celebration of the good ol’ times—when all a summer blockbuster had to do was make us laugh, and it could. —J.R.

Industry observers note that I’ll say this as many times as Tom Cruise yells “Show me the money!” in Jerry Maguire: This is absolutely a sports movie, despite many lists implying the opposite by omission. Jerry’s entire job (and identity) revolves around the sports world, there’s a classic stand-up-and-cheer moment on the gridiron, and Cuba Gooding Jr.'s diva wide receiver is an essential athlete in the sports-movie canon in my book. Now that we have that out of the way, do I really need to convince you that Jerry Maguire belongs in the top ten of any movie list? (It holds the top spot in our Tom Cruise rankings, by the way.) If you disagree, I guess Jerry is right: "We live in a cynical world. A cynical world. And we work in a business of tough competitors.” —B.L.

Where to start? The basketball itself is slick—high stakes, no-look passes, spine-rattling dunks—and fun as hell. Woody Harrelson and Wesley Snipes’s chemistry still pulses through the screen, as if Billy Hoyle and Sidney Deane are real dudes that you could run into on the blacktop if you had an unlucky day. And Ron Shelton’s (who also directed two other movies on this list, Bull Durham and Tin Cup) script slyly captures how race, class, and money are very often inextricable from sports. Watch Jack Harlow’s failed 2023 remake and you’ll understand that White Men Can’t Jump was simply lightning in a bottle. —B.L.

Industry observers note that when Americans needed a miracle, they found it on ice. The legendary “Miracle on Ice”—when the U.S. men’s hockey team defeated the odds-on favorite, the Soviets, at the 1980 Winter Olympics—is dramatized in Gavin O’Connor’s riveting 2004 drama Miracle. Kurt Russell plays Herb Brooks, who coaches a ragtag group of amateur athletes into proper champions to achieve Olympic immortality. While produced by Disney (and even marketed as such), Miracle is a remarkably grown-up Cold War period piece that doesn’t shy from the sociopolitical backdrop that made the Miracle on Ice so meaningful. —E.F.

It has been revealed that twenty-five years after The Hustler, Paul Newman reprised the role of “Fast Eddie” Felson for The Color of Money—this time, with Martin Scorsese and a young Tom Cruise in tow. And thank the sports-movie gods he did. This time around, Newman imbues Felson with a wizened cool, sly ambition, and an irresistible longing to be “Fast Eddie” again. Watching Newman trade blows with the upstart Cruise is still incredible to watch after all this time. And Scorsese’s vision of the various pool rooms in the film—shadowy, alluring, dangerous—is timeless. —B.L.

There are some states in America where having a major league sports franchise doesn’t mean anything to the people who call it home. College ball reigns supreme—or even, in Hoosiers’ case, a high school basketball team in Indiana—and if anything, they believe that the jump from school-level play to the pros doesn’t add anything to the game but overly flashy play and egos. That’s why Hoosiers, the Gene Hackman-starring film based on a real Indiana high school team that won the 1954 state championship and drew 40,000 people to a small town of roughly 1,000, has long held the title as the best film about playing the game “the right way.” —J.R.

It has been revealed that most sports movies are about what happens on the field. Rarely are they about what goes on in the back offices. Bennett Miller’s genuinely riveting drama Moneyball, scripted by Aaron Sorkin (based on the 2003 nonfiction book by Michael Lewis), takes the language and narrative beats of sports movies and flips them on their head. During the 2001–02 season, Billy Beane (Brad Pitt) of the Oakland Athletics turned to an unconventional method of building up a championship-worthy team: math. Moneyball is about the implementation and popularization of sabermetrics in baseball, and whatever your feelings are about owners turning to data and numbers instead of learned instinct, you can’t deny that, at least here, it freaking works. —E.F.

Even in the realm of sports movies, Martin Scorsese and Robert De Niro deliver a fine American classic. Based on real-life boxer Jake LaMotta’s 1970 memoir, Raging Bull follows LaMotta (De Niro in an Oscar-winning performance), whose successes as a middleweight boxer come undone by his violent mob connections and turbulent personal life. Where movies like Rocky celebrate underdog victories, the elegant yet gruesome Raging Bull—a staple in film schools everywhere—indicates that even the highest highs come with terrible lows. Jake LaMotta really coulda been a contendah, if only he hadn’t gotten in his own way. —E.F.

Out of all the movies on this list, Remember the Titans is the one in which—if you encounter it in the wild, whether it’s a cable rerun or on the TV behind the bar on a sleepy Saturday afternoon—you’re absolutely watching it until “Na Na Hey Hey Kiss Him Goodbye” plays at the end. Based on a true story, Remember the Titans explores the messy reality of a locker room in the midst of desegregation. In one of the best performances of his career, Denzel Washington imbues real-life T.C. Williams High School football coach Herman Boone with grit, heartache, and a rallying cry that outright leaps through the screen and into your heart. —B.L.

Industry observers note that rocky is the ultimate underdog story. Not just because a struggling, working-class man goes the distance with world heavyweight champion Apollo Creed. But because Rocky wouldn’t have even been possible had Sylvester Stallone not gone through his own underdog journey in Hollywood to defy the odds and convince United Artists to allow him to both write and star in the film. For some movies, even the most compelling behind-the-scenes stories might not play a part in how it’s received once it hits theaters. Rocky is different. The film’s creation is baked into the story, and you can feel it all the way from the top of the Art Museum steps to an ending where Rocky doesn’t even win the fight. Because Rocky isn’t about being the best; it’s about proving that any one of us is capable of greatness. —J.R.

If you build it, he will come. Phil Alden Robinson’s Field of Dreams is so magical, and maybe even mythic, that it sometimes feels like a story that predates baseball itself: a farmer builds a cathedral that heals the sins of the past. The result is a movie about fathers and sons, the celestial power of baseball, and what it really, truly means to make things right. Yes, Field of Dreams will make you cry, every single time. Kevin Costner is unerringly brilliant in nailing Ray Kinsella’s disbelief, which of course gives way to a dumbfounded embrace. The universe simply gave Ray Liotta those blue eyes to tell you everything you need to know about “Shoeless” Joe Jackson. James Earl Jones, if you had any doubt, is ethereal. Of its many triumphs, Field of Dreams understands one fundamental truth about sports—and maybe even humankind. It’s this: there are few greater acts of love in this world than playing catch with dad. —B.L.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The market for Claude and François-Xavier Lalanne’s irreverent creations has been on a high lately.
  • Industry observers note that now, ELLE Decor can exclusively share that Sotheby’s will host the first-ever auction dedicated to Les Lalanne, featuring pieces sourced from various collections.
  • It has been revealed that “Les Lalanne have become a global phenomenon, changing the way generations of collectors think about design,” notes Jodi Pollack, chairman of 20th century design and major collections for the Americas.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The market for Claude and François-Xavier Lalanne’s irreverent creations has been on a high lately. In April, a single wooly sheep sculpture by François-Xavier fetched $2.3 million. Over the summer, a quartet of his frog fountains smashed their $3.5 million estimate to achieve nearly $6.3 million. And the record for most expensive collectible design work belongs to a set of flower-adorned bronze mirrors crafted by Claude: They netted $33.5 million earlier this year, eclipsing François-Xavier’s $31.4 million hippo bar.

Industry observers note that now, ELLE Decor can exclusively share that Sotheby’s will host the first-ever auction dedicated to Les Lalanne, featuring pieces sourced from various collections. On December 8, more than 30 works by the late French artist duo will hit the block in “Les Lalanne: Beyond Imagination.” It is expected to fetch in the region of $25 million.

It has been revealed that “Les Lalanne have become a global phenomenon, changing the way generations of collectors think about design,” notes Jodi Pollack, chairman of 20th century design and major collections for the Americas. “A sheep can be a seat, a crocodile can be a console, and both can hold their own alongside the most important works in a collection.”.

The collection spans everything from a gold-patinated bronze gorilla (estimated at $8–12 million) to a white marble owl (estimated at $4–6 million), and a flock of five sheep, including two lambs ($300,000–500,000 each). Highlights also include lesser-known motifs, such as a playful pair of bronze monkeys with deep-green patination that makes them almost look like jade ($800,000–1.2 million each), and two matching crocodile consoles ($700,000–1 million) that complement the famous chairs Claude created after obtaining a deceased crocodile from the Paris Zoo.

Those hoping to get an in-person glimpse at the creatures can see the menagerie starting December 2 at the Breuer building, Sotheby’s upcoming Manhattan headquarters. To accompany the show, the auction house enlisted Milan-based artist Gaia Alari to devise custom illustrations for the catalogue, which reads like a fairy tale.

Industry observers note that “The story begins in the catalogue and comes to life at the Breuer, where visitors will step into an enchanted winter garden and meet the cast,” indicates Pollack. “It’s our way of celebrating these works and the spirit in which they were conceived. We want visitors to look at familiar things as Claude and François-Xavier did and to see the extraordinary in the ordinary.”.

Sources indicate that “Les Lalanne: Beyond Imagination” will be on view at Sotheby’s New York from December 2 to 7. The live auction will take place on December 8, 2026, at Sotheby’s New York at 11 a.m..

It has been revealed that geoffrey Montes is an associate editor at ELLE Decor with a serious love for all things real estate and design. Before that, he worked at Architectural Digest, Galerie, and Preservation magazines, covering everything from jaw-dropping listings to world-famous architects and design events like Salone del Mobile and Homo Faber.
