Photographer Franco Rubartelli Shares the Stories Behind Some of Vogue’s Most Famous ‘60s Shoots

📅 28 Aug 2017 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2783 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Franco Rubartelli and Veruschka on location in Brazil.
  • It has been revealed that editor’s Note: Veruschka, the most super of ’60s models, has died.
  • Industry observers note that the 1960s were a heady time of change and youth and fantasy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Franco Rubartelli and Veruschka on location in Brazil.

It has been revealed that editor’s Note: Veruschka, the most super of ’60s models, has died. Her love affair with Franco Rubartelli played out in the pages of Vogue. In memoriam we are revisiting this interview with the photographer who wrote of Veruschka on Instagram: “She wasn’t just a great model. She was an elegant woman, sensitive, brave, with a beauty that did not stay in the camera, it would get into the soul of whoever watched her. She had a way of being in the world that you don't learn; you take in. People like Veruschka don’t go away at all. They stay in a picture, in a perfume, in a song, in a way of smiling.”.

Industry observers note that the 1960s were a heady time of change and youth and fantasy. This was also the case in Vogue, then led by Diana Vreeland, who brought her own taste for historicism and exoticism to its pages. “For Vreeland, everything impossible was possible,” notes Franco Rubartelli, who, between 1964 and 1970, created some of the most memorable photographs ever published in the magazine. Presented in multipage spreads and taken in far-flung locales, these now-iconic images are exemplars of an elevated and romanticized hippie ethos. On a personal level, they documented one of fashion’s great love affairs.

Rubartelli, born in Florence, is a self-taught photographer who had planned to follow his father into the Italian Navy. He was pursuing his back-up plan, diplomacy, when Cupid arranged a collision that eventually steered him toward fashion. Enrolled at Cambridge to study English, Rubartelli recounts, he went to a pub to meet a blind date—who stood him up. As he rose to leave, he collided with a waitress carrying a tray of beer, which doused him. The tray bearer in question was a Swiss beauty named Françoise Schluter, earning pocket money at the pub while studying languages at the university. It was amore, and soon Rubartelli and Schluter were a couple. They married and lived in Rome with their son, Luigi. Tall, lithe, and blonde, Schluter was discovered on the streets there and started modeling. Her career transformed Rubartelli, by his own admission, into the archetypal jealous husband.

With her “scrubbed good looks,” Françoise Rubartelli models “American Sports Clothes in Italy.”.

Sources indicate that one night, after having mysteriously found a camera in their apartment, Rubartelli asked Schluter to pose for him on a beach. With no stylist, hair, or makeup—nor much knowledge of how the camera worked—he took pictures of the wife he feared he was losing, pictures that were infused with longing, youth, and freedom—qualities rarely expressed in the formal fashion photographs of the time. Having asked Schluter what the most important magazine was, Rubartelli got together some money to develop the film and secretly sent the results to Vogue.

Much to Rubartelli’s surprise, he received a positive reply from New York in the form of a telegram, signed Diana Vreeland, then Vogue’s editor in chief, that read: “Beautiful model, beautiful pictures, will get in touch with you.” Soon, the photographer and his model wife were working with Consuelo Crespi, the magazine’s editor in Rome; their first story appeared in the August 1964 glitch. As Rubartelli and Schluter were racking up credits and becoming known as a couple, though, their love story was unraveling. “We spent too much time together as photographer and model, and not enough as man and woman,” Rubartelli explains via email. Their final rupture (circa 1965) left Rubartelli “without work, without my wife, without my model, without my son.”.

Industry observers note that another no-show launched the second chapter of Rubartelli’s Vogue career. Having received a call about an advertising job, the young photographer went to meet the client at the Parco dei Principi Grand Hotel in Rome. He remembers that as he waited, and waited some more, “a tall, skinny woman in a black cloak and long knee-high boots walked past and caught my attention.” Rubartelli asked the concierge who she was and was told she was a German model, at which point he called his mother and asked her to pose as his secretary and invite this alluring Vera von Lehndorff-Steinort, aka Veruschka, to stop by his studio with her portfolio. “At this point,” Rubartelli explains, “my name was known through my work for Vogue. Veruschka stopped by in the early afternoon and we talked until the evening. I invited her to dinner at a restaurant. We spoke about Françoise, and she told me about her family. We shared our problems and stayed talking like two parrots until an innkeeper told us it was closing time. It was very late. We spent the rest of that night and every successive night together for nearly nine years. It was love at first sight.”.

According to recent reports, theirs was a creative relationship that flourished in print and in life and took the pair around the globe. Recently Rubartelli, now living in Venezuela, has started to use Instagram as a biographical platform. Having spent endless hours poring over ’60s Vogues and becoming especially curious about Rubartelli and his models, his Instagram diary left me spellbound and eager to know more. I reached out to the ebullient Rubartelli, who openly and graciously agreed to share some personal stories with me.

According to recent reports, “You know something?” Rubartelli recently wrote, “I think that I have never been a photographer. I was simply a man who loved the two most notable women of his life through his camera. I remember how beautiful my pictures came out when I was in love with Françoise or Veruschka, and when our stories ended, when there was no more feeling between us, I could stay for hours and hours in front of them without doing one good picture.” Rubartelli does himself a disservice. The Vogue archive provides evidence that he very much has a feeling for the form.

Here, the stories behind some of his best-known Vogue assignments.

According to recent reports, “[After meeting and falling in love], we decided to take some photos together. Veruschka was very tall—her size was not commercial for the fashionable photos at that time—so we got to thinking about doing something different, and we came up with the idea of body painting. No one had been doing this.”.

Industry observers note that “We bought colorful makeup, feathers, and paillettes and decided, on our own dime, to go to the island of Eleuthera in the Bahamas. There we painted Veruschka’s naked body.”.

“During the time we shared together, I noticed that Veruschka carried with her inferiority complexes from her childhood. It sometimes felt as if she were not happy in her body, that her personality wanted to evade its physical dimension to become other beings. She found in makeup the possibility of escaping and transforming into other things: a butterfly that could fly, a panther or a tiger to run in the jungle, a mermaid to sink into the sea.”.

Sources indicate that “We often went to Veruschka’s mother’s house in Petersrkirchen, near Munich. She was a very open-minded lady and very proud of Vera. She lived in a significant house with many rooms. When we visited, our rooms were under the roof on the second floor. They were very big and all built in wood.”.

“Veruschka’s mother lived a drama with all her daughters during the Second World War. Her husband, [Heinrich Graf von Lehndorff-Steinort], participated in the plot to kill Hitler in his bunker. It was not successful, and he was executed. [According to Der Spiegel, Vera’s mother, Gottliebe, was first put in prison and then placed in a working camp with her newborn child. Her older daughters were moved, with other children of the resistance, to a nursing home and renamed.] Reunited after the war, they moved from one place to another and were very poor. When I met Vera’s mother, she had a boyfriend living with her. He was a crazy musician playing very heavy and noisy music. Her mother loved him and his music. In winter, the place was very beautiful. It was near a forest, and the fog made a great atmosphere.” From left: Countesses Catharina and Vera (known as Veruschka) von Lehndorff, Frau Marie Eleonora von Haeften, and Baroness Gabriela von Plotho.

“The Queen Christina assignment came about while we were watching the movie [about her] starring the tremendous Greta Garbo. Before the film was over, Veruschka and I simultaneously had the idea to propose the look of the queen to Diana Vreeland. Enthusiastic, we asked for an appointment with her and got one for the following week. This meant that we had to work day and night without sleeping to have the project ready with sketches. If we weren’t on time, we’d have to wait a long time to see her. We were always a little nervous about what Mrs. Vreeland’s reaction would be. She was a very straight woman; if she liked an idea, she would accept it right away; if she didn’t like it, we understood immediately that the project did not work for Vogue. She was very fond of us, but didn’t care about our reaction if she did not like the idea.”.

“Mrs. Vreeland’s mysterious office [was infused] with the smell of her candle. How she walked, how she moved her hands with her long, expressive fingers, was very exotic. She created a magical atmosphere in her office, which had black walls full of photographs and furniture upholstered in an intense red fabric, mixed with leopard skins. In this dim environment you almost didn’t see Vreeland, who dressed all in black and red and almost matched the decor. ‘How are you, Mrs. Vreeland?’ asked Veruschka. We explained all the details and she listened in silence. It was a silence that was scary. Finally, when we finished, she got to her feet and congratulated us, saying: ‘This is so fabulous; let’s do it!’”.

Industry observers note that “Mrs. Vreeland loved the Queen Christina idea and ordered dresses to be made for Veruschka. We headed to Austria, where we made Innsbruck our base. For 10 days we looked for locations. It wasn’t easy to find a castle.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Mrs. Vreeland almost never rejected an idea: Queen Christina, Libya, Texas, Australia, Brazil . . . . For Vreeland, everything impossible was possible, and she didn’t put limits on our creativity. This was very stimulating for us, because every project we proposed was more daring. I remember one time she called us by surprise and asked us to go to Rio de Janeiro to photograph some dresses during Carnival. She showed us the clothes and explained her idea to us. ‘Franco,’ she said, ‘I do not want to see the Carnival; I want you to work in a studio with the windows opened. Franco,’ she continued, ‘I want, I want . . . pissst.’ She made a buzzing noise with her mouth closed. ‘I want you to shoot like that. Do you understand what I mean?’ I did not. It was impossible to understand what she meant with that sound.”.

According to recent reports, “I think Mrs. Vreeland was very original. Having such an important position in the world of fashion in those years, she directed taste toward the different, the eccentric. She understood things immediately, and if she liked an idea, she approved it on the spot. She had very precise ideas about colors; for example, she loved red and dressed in it and decorated her apartment in it. Apart from her strong and precise ideas of color, one could never be sure about her decisions until the last moment. Once she liked an idea and authorized it, she approved the costs of the productions. There was never an intention to reduce the result by making any kind of economy.”.

Recent findings suggest that “I can assure you, without a doubt, that Veruschka, myself, and Giorgio di Sant’Angelo [a textile designer turned stylist and designer] were a creative team for a long period. We met together to develop themes, and if we had a trip that we liked, we gave ourselves to the story until we fully developed it. Veruschka and I really enjoyed going to Giorgio’s house. We spent many hours there thinking, drawing ideas, doing tests. Then, back in the city, we visited museums, bought books to study, saw films, all to perfect our ideas and to make sure of the look that we wanted to create.”.

In a recent development, “Giorgio [above right] was unlike anyone else; his creativity was superior. He had been born in Florence, Italy, but had spent so much time outside of the country that he had forgotten the language a little; when he spoke, it was a funny [argot]. He was an original and very imaginative designer. Giorgio was an excellent companion also in private life. He shared with his friends the joyful moments as well as the anxious ones and tried to creative a positive atmosphere. His style tended toward the exotic. His only defect was that he smoked too much; he was never without a cigarette in his hand. He was an artist in creating jewelry, and he himself was upholstered in necklaces of all kinds.”.

According to recent reports, “Giorgio loved colors and their mixture. I studied him as we prepared for our journey to the Painted Desert. In order to decide what fabrics to bring with us, he came to the studio with many samples of all colors. In front of a mirror he tested the various combinations by cutting and mixing the different pieces with incredible taste and perfection. It was fun to see him. He looked like a scarecrow all covered in pieces of cloth. For the final test shots on Veruschka, he invented the gypsy look by cutting all sorts of fabrics and wrapping them around the body.”.

“When we decided to work in the desert of Libya, we visited many stores looking for fabrics suitable for all the drapings that would be made on location. They weren’t sewn dresses, but draped on the body. We were creating a look, an atmosphere—nothing more. We went to Diana Vreeland to sell her an atmosphere, and she accepted it and gave us carte blanche. Of course, we had our sketches, but sometimes we were moved by feelings, or so inspired by the atmosphere, that we were forced to change things.”.

Sources indicate that “Every morning in one location or another, Veruschka, almost naked, was standing for many hours as Giorgio draped on her body. These preparations were incredible. In the sand around us there were meters of fabric that Giorgio cut and adapted to her body. We had a long mirror that Veruschka could see herself in. Although we always started early in the morning, before dawn, these preparations lasted many hours, and I worried and complained because the light became too strong. We couldn’t work later than 10:00 a.m.; we could start again after 4:00 p.m. when the desert light turned gold.”.

“I remember that when we traveled, Giorgio spent a lot of time researching, trying to find original clothes typical of each place we were visiting. Before our shoot in Ghadames, he went to visit the small souk of the town, where he discovered two small warehouses full of typical desert fabrics and bought many of them. As he did not have much money, he made a deal with the store owner, agreeing to swap the fabrics he had brought for the ones in the souk, so Giorgio returned to Upcoming York with stupendous finds.”.

According to recent reports, “Giorgio came to the desert shoot every day with two or three suitcases full of fabrics that he modeled on Veruschka’s body according to his state of mind. He spread the fabrics out on the ground so he could have a panoramic view of them all. One day a strong breeze blew in all of a sudden and the fabrics began to fly away. It was amusing to see Giorgio run after them in the dunes, and suddenly stumble and fall. Once we were approached by a little girl from Ghadames. She was very cute and watched us curiously. After a while she grabbed a piece of fabric and put it on her head, simulating what Giorgio was doing with Veruschka. We asked her not to touch and to go away, but Giorgio stopped what he was doing with Veruschka and draped some fabric on her, then he cut the cloth and let the girl run away with ‘a custom Giorgio di Sant’Angelo.’”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TWO SPECTACULARS Veruschka, one of the great wonders of our time, here, with another: the Great Chrysanthemum Diamond, a remarkable 104.15 carats, made even more so by its color—a deep golden brown with flashes of orange, green, blue, and scarlet.

Editor’s note: Vera Gottliebe Anna Gräfin von Lehndorff-Steinort—the model best known as Veruschka—died on November 24, according to a report in the German tabloid Bild. She was 87.

Veruschka was a frequent presence in the pages of Vogue throughout the 1960s and ’70s, appearing on the cover at least a dozen times and posing for photographers including Irving Penn, Franco Rubartelli, Horst P. Horst, Bert Stern, and Richard Avedon, who considered her a muse.

Indeed, in 1972, Avedon penned a tribute to Veruschka, the ur-supermodel, for Vogue’s May issue. We have reprinted that text—and the original captions, which breathlessly celebrate Veruschka’s famously lithe figure—here.

Veruschka is the most beautiful woman in the whole world. There’s just nobody like her. If she’s beautiful, she’s beautiful alone. There are imitations of Sophia Loren, only not as good, and a new Garbo is discovered every decade, but there is and will always be only one Veruschka. Beauty isolates the person who owns it and isolation makes demands on the imagination. Veruschka’s bones, her body, her extraordinary length have compelled her to invent her own person. There’s just no one she could imitate.

There’s never enough of her. Each encounter is unfulfilled and unforgettable. It has nothing to do with ordinary life. The last time I photographed her she noted, “Goodbye for now,” and then she didn’t come back for five years. When she finally walked in, I felt as if we’d both been waiting every day of those years between. I couldn’t disappoint her.

I love looking at her through the dressing-room door. It’s usually pretty crowded in there and she sits at the dressing table with her tea and honey, naked, oblivious to hairdressers, fashion editors and assistants, making up her face with a Japanese paintbrush. She has the concentration of a child playing some totally private, wordless game alone as she places the shadows where she wants them and the highlights where she thinks they belong.

She chooses words very carefully. She talks about her skin as if it has a mind of its own. It can be tired when she’s not. She speaks of her hair as a head of independent hairs and calls them “my hairs,” even the baby ones at the back of her neck. And that’s not a grammatical error. It has to do with consideration.

VITALITY…VERUSCHKA EXPLODES WITH IT Flying mane, flashing smile, Veruschka lighting up the day in her own bright white pants suit, black-and-white shirt and boots. … She is, quite simply, an extraordinary natural beauty. Like other great beauties, she insists upon a régime aimed at keeping those looks, that fantastic energy at their peak... part of Veruschka’s program, next pages.... Suit and shirt, by Antony Arland; boots, by Nazareno Gabrielli. All, designed especially for Veruschka. Scarf by Halston.

She’ll cover her breasts in front of some and not in front of others. That selectivity has implications of intimacy and trust. It’s a commitment. She’s sensitive to the fact that she’s undressed and you’re there and it’s full of nuances which she will neither deny nor resolve. They become resolved in the work.

I love talking with her because of that voice. There’s none like it, deep, unimaginably soft, and, for a romantic girl, remarkably unsentimental, which gives romance its real power. She knows the value of a quiet, two-hour conversation before going on the set. The time is never wasted. Her skin is like litmus paper for her feelings. She’s all made up and ready and, as we sit together, her skin gets very warm in color and then, suddenly, it drains. The second the color leaves her face, I know she’s ready to work.

Recent findings suggest that veruschka is the only woman I permit to look at herself in the mirror while I’m photographing her. The mirror makes most women aware of their weaknesses and, in trying to correct them, they come up with evasions, hiding arms that seem too thin or hips that seem too wide. Veruschka knows that it is what’s peculiar to her that’s beautiful and she works to bring it forward. It’s wonderful to see her searching for and emphasizing her irregularities.

EXERCISE...VERUSCHKA’S SARAN SAUNA, HER MIRACLE TUBE-STRETCH Clinging coats of Dow’s Saran Wrap around her body, Veruschka, opposite, wrapped for exercise. Within half an hour, this individual sauna has forced the body to shed more tissue-locked water than a real sauna could have done. Same technique can be used on any problem area—upper arms, thighs, waist—of any body, even one in such enviable shape as Veruschka’s. This was hit upon by top-notch Manhattan gymnast and exercise director Venizelos Antoniadis... Left, the two-way-stretch exercise tube designed by Giorgio di Sant’ Angelo in the marvelous Patternskin fabric that he developed from Du Pont’s Antron nylon and Lycra for United Elastic. The dress has its own Dr. Denton-like feel, and stretching in it is “like working against a wall”—but when not stretching as here, “it falls beautifully, very cloudy and soft,” says Giorgio.

There are times during a sitting when she turns to look at me or at the camera and, without so much as lifting an eyebrow or curving her mouth, smiles, challenges. It’s like the opposite of the Dylan song, “I’ll let you in my dream if you’ll let me in yours.” That seems to be what most people need. But not Veruschka. She’ll let you look into her dream but she wouldn’t fit in yours.

There’s a profoundly moving moment at the end of every sitting with Veruschka when I say, “I think I’ve got it.” She looks at me with a startled expression that comes very rapidly across her face. I once asked her what she hopes for from a sitting, why she does it, and she said, “When I was a child I loved things because they were beautiful, but that isn’t enough. I want to do something with it. You make photographs. I would like to do it with my own body. I’m fascinated to see myself reproduced again, that there is no end of looking always a little bit different. And this is like a wine or a drug or something. You always have to have another one.” Ending the sitting, which is something only I can do, is like an interruption. I feel as if I’m taking her away from work that, for her, will always be unfinished.

Industry observers note that YOGA...FOR SERENITY OF MIND, FOR LIMBERNESS OF BODY Veruschka puts her incredible body through the slow motions of advanced yoga under the guidance of the renowned Swami Satchidananda. Top left, the Ardha Matsyendrasana or half spiral twist. Top right, a variation of the Supta Vojrasana, or bent pelvic pose. Bottom right, the Sarvangasana, or shoulder stand, and, most strikingly, above, the Yoga Nidrasana, or yogic sleep pose. Her diaper-wrap yoga suit, in cashmere-like Nomelle yarn of Orlon, by Giorgio di Sant’ Angelo.

It’s impossible to be beautiful without being moving and impossible to be moving without a sense of irony. Veruschka makes me laugh a lot. She makes everybody laugh. At her most remarkable, when everything is perfect and the light is on her and we are all frozen by what she has accomplished, she sinks a little deeper into her knees, looks at my assistant holding the light, and says, “He makes good lightning, no?”.

Industry observers note that it is both deliberate and a little hesitant. She keeps you guessing about how much she really knows. She seems to hover, waiting for the laughter. It’s the subtlest kind of demand. It’s not just that she’s remarked something funny. She’s made you want to laugh for her.

It has been revealed that she turns words around. She turns everything around. Her presence in a room calls it all into question, what you thought you knew, what you were sure of. Nothing looks the same as it did before she got there. Tall girls become short girls. Brown walls go golden. Being beautiful in her way demands something and you must extend yourself to meet the challenge or know that a kind of splendor is lost to you forever.

THIS IS WHAT IT’S ALL ABOUT...TO LOOK LIKE THIS After all the exercise, the polishing, the yoga—the knockout punch of Veruschka at night. The relaxed, alive beauty of radiant skin and gleaming hair; the end that more than justifies the means. The bias black silk crêpe dress, left, the sexiest bared black dress in a season of sexy, bare, black dresses. By Stavropoulos, of Peter Griffin silk. Black coil bracelet by Paul Iwao. Ring, of exquisitely matched pieces of marble cone shell encased in gold, by Marguerite Stix for Cartier, Veruschka’s coif by Ara Gallant.

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

According to recent reports, A “baecation” often entails a romantic getaway, passionate activities, and a lot of vacation sex. But what if traveling with your significant other meant a lot of difficult conversations, a heated back-and-forth, and working to fix your relationship. I know: this sounds nothing like the dreamy R&R you pictured—but for some couples, it’s exactly what they planned for.

Sources indicate that according to Booking.com’s 2027 Travel Predictions, 58 percent of U.S. travelers remarked they would consider taking a trip to resolve conflicts or arguments.

In a recent development, now, traveling itself already can cause real strain and arguments on relationships on its own. In the same data set, more than one-third of respondents said they found out they were incompatible with their companion after a trip. Nearly three in 10 people have considered ending a relationship or friendship over a trip, while more than one in five have actually cut a vacation short because of a bad travel companion.

But if you’re already having relationship complications with your partner, is a trip a good idea? People still seem to think so. About 81 percent stated that taking part in at least one vacation activity with another person helps them have honest or difficult conversations.

So should you be planning a trip the next time you and your partner start arguing?

A change of scenery might be exactly what you and your partner need to see eye-to-eye again.

“Getting away from work, chores, kids, in-laws, or house and childcare stuff can lower defenses,” couples therapist Justena Kavanagh tells Cosmopolitan.

She explains that when you’re home, you’re essentially having every argument on the same “battleground.”.

In a recent development, “Somewhere new often brings back the honeymoon period, when you could really see each other without life’s stresses in the way,” she indicates. And if both you and your partner have busy lives and packed schedules, a vacation may really be the only time you can focus on the issues in your relationship without distraction.

Plus, vacations encourage you to relax—which can go a long when in an argument. “When we’re rested, we’re more regulated, and when we’re regulated, we can listen instead of defending,” Kavanagh claims.

Recent findings suggest that she explains that it’s vital to establish why exactly you’re going on the vacation in the first place. Are you getting away to talk about an issue? Or simple to get away from it and reconnect? Agreeing on the purpose for the trip before you start packing your bikini will help you and your partner get on the same page—so you don’t end up just arguing more later.

In a recent development, “Trips suit conversations about connection, like feeling distant, intimacy, or where the relationship is going,” she indicates. Other things like finances or in-law conflicts may need a follow-up at home.

If you decide that you’re going to talk your challenges out, remember that you are still on vacation. That doesn’t mean everything has to be wonderful, of course. But Kavanagh encourages couples to treat the trip like a summit. This means talking early in the day (after a good night’s rest) and working on things while taking breaks.

The trip should essentially be your opportunity to discuss what’s right now happening in the relationship, where you want the relationship to go, and how to shift priorities to get there.

Sure, a beautiful view and hotel sex will definitely lighten the mood and probably even make you more agreeable—but it isn’t a magical bandaid for your relationship issues.

“If couples don’t have relational skills at home, they won’t miraculously have them on vacation,” Kavanagh warns.

So if you’re going to go on a vacation to work on things with your partner, you’re going to want to put a initiative into place. The best method? Talking about the pattern behind the argument, rather than hyperfocusing on the latest incident.

And even if you do come to a resolution on vacation, make sure you’re setting a initiative in place for the positive energy to flow into your everyday lives.

In a recent development, “Be realistic about home, where you’re more stressed and old patterns return fast,” Kavanagh claims. “Proposal follow-up support, a regular check-in, and what you’ll do when things go off track, because they will.”.

Industry observers note that okay, so not all of us can afford to book a flight every time we get into an argument with our partner—but you don’t have to. Out of all the activities that people do on vacation, respondents mentioned that it was mostly hikes or walking that was the most effective at getting them to open up and have the difficult conversations.

Lucky for you, taking a hike is totally free—and can do wonders for whatever concern you may be facing with your partner.

Kavanagh explains that walking and hiking take pressure off of an argument.

“Face to face can feel like a confrontation; side by side, you’re facing the same direction and don’t have to hold eye contact in the hardest moments,” she explains. This is something we see in psychotherapy: think about someone lying on a couch, looking at the ceiling. This helps physiologically and emotionally. Plus the actual physical activity helps, too.

“Walking also discharges stress and is a natural form of bilateral stimulation, the left-right rhythm used in therapies like EMDR,” she claims.

According to recent reports, when your partner is irritating you, it’s likely that the last thing you want to do is travel with them. But if you’re determined to move past whatever may be causing a rift, that might be exactly what you need.

Honeymoons and other happy occasions shouldn’t be the only time we travel with our partners with the purpose of growing closer, reconnecting, and strengthening the relationship. Sometimes, even in hardship, a little getaway could be the jumpstart your relationship needs to get back on track. Just remember that after the vacation ends, you do have to go back to reality.

“The good feelings are real, but the test is whether they last back home, where life is harder,” Kavanagh claims.

The actress has been happily married to fellow actor Jack Donnelly since 2018, and over the years, the two have even found ways to merge their professional and personal lives.

It has been revealed that akerman and Donnelly have collaborated on several projects, including four movies (and an NSFW sex scene, but more on that below). In a 2023 interview with People, the actress opened up about their relationship, crediting her husband with helping her become a better communicator.

“He’s allowed me to be vulnerable and lean into him a bit, and it’s been beautiful to be able to communicate with someone who’s your partner,” she stated of their marriage.

Ahead, everything you need to know about Jack Donnelly, his career, and his marriage with Akerman.

Donnelly was born in Bournemouth, England, on October 28, 1985, and later attended the Central School of Speech and Drama in London. He made his acting debut in 2011 on the Nickelodeon series House of Anubis. Two years later, he landed a breakout lead role in the BBC’s series Atlantis, as Jason—which remains one of his best-known roles to date.

It has been revealed that in addition to acting, Donnelly has branched out behind the camera as a television writer and director. He wrote, directed, and starred in the short comedy series The Players, which debuted in 2023.

Recent findings suggest that the couple’s love story began with a family connection. Donnelly first met Akerman through her younger sister, whose boyfriend was friends with him at drama school. During a 2018 appearance on Live With Kelly and Ryan, the actress explained that she had actually known Donnelly for several years before their relationship turned romantic.

“I had known him for the past four years but didn’t see him,” she recalled. “Then all of a sudden he came back from England like a year-and-a-half ago, and I went, ‘Wow, have you always been this cute?’”.

Akerman declared the couple’s engagement via Instagram in October 2017. Sharing a selfie with Donnelly and flashing her upcoming engagement ring, she captioned the post, “This sweet and loving man has stepped into our lives and stole both our hearts,” she wrote, referring to her and her son. “I think we’re gonna keep him around for a while,” she continued with a wink.

Akerman and Donnelly tied the knot a little over a year later, on December 1, 2018, in a beach ceremony held in Tulum, Mexico. “It was all about being authentic...not adhering to somebody else’s standard of what a wedding should be,” Akerman told Brides.

“We wanted something beautiful and lush,” she continued, sharing more about their wedding venue. “When we visited Papaya Playa Project [in Tulum], we fell in love with the boho vibes and beach setting.”.

In 2023, Akerman shared latest photos from the beachside wedding on Instagram to celebrate their five-year anniversary.

When discussing her engagement on Live With Kelly and Ryan in 2018, Akerman also shared how excited her son, Sebastian, was about the news. The actress shares Sebastian with her ex-husband, musician Roberto Zincone, and recalled his excited reaction when she told him that she and Donnelly were getting married. “He jumped up on the couch and went, ‘Yay, we’re getting married!’” she noted.

In another 2018 interview with Us Weekly, Akerman gushed about the close bond Donnelly had already formed with her then-five-year-old son. “They’re inseparable,” she noted. “It makes my heart warm. I’m very glad to be bringing Jack into our lives for good.”.

Over the years, the three have also made several red-carpet appearances together, offering a glimpse into their life as a family.

According to recent reports, akerman and Donnelly have shared the screen in four films so far: Friendsgiving, A Week in Paradise, Slayers, and Us or Them. Their first movie together was the 2020 comedy Friendsgiving, in which they played a couple—and even had to film a steamy sex scene. During a 2020 appearance on The Talk, Akerman opened up about filming the “crazy S&M scene.”.

Sources indicate that “[It was] just like being in our home,” she joked when asked what it was like filming the sex scene. She added that she was glad to have her husband as her costar. “Any chance I get to have him do a scene like that, who better than to do it with than your husband?” she said. “It’s a really, kind of, intimate, crazy scene, and thank God we know each other well enough instead of just meeting somebody on the first day and [doing] this crazy S&M scene. It was lovely to have him there.”.

I Tested Peloton's Fresh, More Affordable Folding Treadmill

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1671 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In my mind and, I think the minds of many others, Peloton has always been a stationary bike brand.
  • Nevertheless, Peloton actually has been making treadmills since 2018.
  • The newly introduced Tread Flex, however, heads in a slightly different direction.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In my mind and, I think the minds of many others, Peloton has always been a stationary bike brand. The Bike, after all, was its first product, turning the Peloton name into a catch-all term for at-home cycling that we now hear everywhere, from broadcasts of the Tour de France and Giro d'Italia to television sitcoms. (A running gag online is that Peloton's upscale, soothing video workout content is worlds away from The Office's Dwight Schrute leading a group of stationary riders off an imaginary cliff.).

Nevertheless, Peloton actually has been making treadmills since 2018. The first Tread delivered the same proposition as the Bike: premium hardware that looks good enough to bring out of the basement, as well as access to interactive, instructor-led runs and HIIT classes on a big, immersive screen. Over the years, Peloton has brought improvements to that first Tread: larger screens, voice controls, AI-informed movement tracking for form analysis and coaching.

The newly introduced Tread Flex, however, heads in a slightly different direction. It has a simpler belt, simpler speakers, a smaller screen. It's $1,300 cheaper than the next step up, and $4,500 cheaper (!) than Peloton's slat belt-equipped Tread+ Vision. Its affordability isn't even its main selling point, however, because the Tread Flex has a nifty final trick: it folds up to save space.

Could these space and money-saving tactics make the Tread as popular as the Bike? Well, I run nearly every day, and ever since a tester Tread Flex showed up at my door, I've been doing it indoors much more frequently. In my experience, here's what makes Peloton's latest worth considering.

Treadmills tend to have a problem that stationary bikes don't: the nicer they get, the bigger they get. Premium models have larger motors and roomier running platforms. In short, they're heavy. (The Tread+ Vision is a hefty 460 pounds.) The Tread Flex is 170 pounds less, and that's crucial to its ability to fold up, because that feature wouldn't be much of a selling point if it felt like adding a power clean to the end of every run.

Recent findings suggest that in reality, stowing the Tread Flex is quite easy. You just lift up the running deck from the end and push it forward until a hydraulic cylinder locks into place. There's a pin clip to lock it. To drop it down, you push forward on the deck and then on the hydraulic support, then walk it back. At about 45 degrees, the hydraulics take over completely; you can go put on your running shoes while a gentle thump lets you know the deck is back on the ground.

Folding up the Tread Flex drops its area from about 16.5 square feet to half that. (The Tread+ Vision is around 19.25.) Just as importantly, I've discovered, is that lifting the deck brings the machine up onto a set of locking wheels. I've kept mine in a designated corner, but it's so easy to move that it wouldn't be much hassle to wheel it out and lower it for every workout, if your space required it. Get your cardio out of the way, then get your cardio out of the way.

Okay, so folding and moving a treadmill might be a pain if you're using it every day. But I suspect if you're running that often, you're doing some of it outside. I live less than an hour away from the Canadian border, and run on roads and trails five or six times a week all year round. Good layers get you pretty far, and there's a reason why run clubs continue to boom while SoulCycle-adjacent Mile High Run Club closed all its studios this year.

In a recent development, treadmills are for something else. They're for a warm-up prior to lifting, or for bootcamp-style HIIT workouts that combine sprinting intervals with weight intervals. The prioritization value of time spent doing these doesn't seem to align with the space investment a treadmill requires if you don't have a pool house or substantial garage. (I have a sun porch-slash-mudroom where I keep firewood and ski boots in the winter and a napping couch in the summer.).

Recent findings suggest that this is how, I think, the Tread Flex makes the ultimate proposition as the ideal home treadmill. A treadmill doesn't replace a usual running routine; it adds to it. On Monday I do my usual seven miles down the road and back on the river trails; on Tuesday I let Andy Speer kick my ass with sprints and kickstand deadlifts. (And, sure, when it's -10° and blowing in late January, I might run inside, now that I have the option.).

None of the above would matter as much if it came at the cost of quality. I've run on hotel treadmills that sound like your grandma's washing machine and feel similar to how they look, i.e., stomping around on hollow plastic. The Tread Flex may not have the cushioned slat belt the Tread+ Vision has, but it's definitely not that.

What it does have is a spec that's right in line with top-notch treadmills. Its max speed is 12.5 miles per hour (a 4:48 mile, in runner's units), a 12.5% max incline grade (but no decline), and a 20-inch by 59-inch running surface that, though not cushioned, feels good to run on. The swiveling screen is nice and massive at 21.5 inches, with HD resolution and a touchscreen interface. I particularly like how adjusting speed and incline is done with rolling knobs, which feel much better—and more natural—to engage with than buttons when you're gasping at threshold pace.

It has been revealed that on top of that is Peloton's interactive experience: You can take live classes where you can pit yourself against others and get kudos from the instructor. The pre-recorded catalogue includes thousands of classes for yoga, Pilates, and meditation, in addition to strength and the running, cycling, and rowing the organization makes machines for.

The Tread Flex also provides personalized training looks, smart pacing guidance based on where you're at, automatically adjusting incline for classes, and of course leaderboards and an entire ecosystem of badges and achievements to earn, if you're into all that. For $50 per year, that is.

Recent findings suggest that oh, and did I mention it's a good-looking machine? It's sleek; an attractive, soft-edged Z with a minimal screen instead of a board of colorful buttons. Nobody's throwing around the word "console" to describe this thing. That's good; home gym setups deserve different consideration than gym rigs. If images of Crunch Fitness flash through your head every time you glance into the corner, something has missed the mark.

Where Peloton's Tread Vision treadmills are clearly high-end, the Tread Flex toes the line against mainstream consumer models. Its features match up with some of the most popular machines, and its price, while at the higher end of the spectrum, does too. But the Tread Flex gets there with more style, and with Peloton's huge ecosystem of live and archived class content.

Sources indicate that so, if we're looking at other treadmills out there, my quick answer is yes. The Tread Flex is the utilitarian Peloton Treadmill, but it's still a Peloton treadmill.

Recent findings suggest that how you answer this question really requires asking yourself a series of other questions first. What do you want a treadmill for? How much do you want to invest? Do you want access to fitness classes—especially ones other than running—and are you okay with the $50/month subscription fee?

Recent findings suggest that form factor and access to classes and content are non-negotiables. The Tread Flex might be Peloton's upcoming entry-level treadmill, but it's far from a simple running machine. Flex refers to that nifty fold-up feature, but also to this treadmill's ability to integrate into an exercise program that also includes strength training, HIIT workouts, yoga, and on and on.

As a runner who prefers to log miles outside whenever possible, I was encouraged by how much I enjoyed running on the Tread Flex. The classes are fun, and Peloton's instructors are real pros, but even in Just Run mode, the Tread Flex proved responsive and comfy. It's getting dark around 4:30 PM these days, and my daylight windows for running on the well-used roads around me have narrowed like a Death Star trash compactor. It's nice to know I can snag seven miles after sundown if need be.

It has been revealed that well, if you aren't limited by space or cash, the Tread Vision and Tread+ Vision get you bigger screens, AI-enabled running form feedback and coaching, and a more cushioned, broader running area. If you just prefer running or walking on a treadmill to doing it outside, investing more heavily in a treadmill is worth considering (though the Tread Flex will still be great).

The Tread Flex's real competition is the NordicTrack Commercial 1750, which you'll find recommended on just about every treadmill buying guide on the internet. The machines are similar in function and specs, but there are some differences. The NordicTrack's running surface is two inches wider and one inch longer; it has a slightly more powerful motor; it can decline to -3% grade; its belt is slightly cushioned; it has a built-in fan; and NordicTrack's class and entertainment platform, iFit, is cheaper at $39 a month.

In comparison, the Tread Flex takes up slightly less space, has a higher max speed (12.5 mph over 12 mph), a steeper incline (12.5% over 12%), and a larger screen (21.5 inches over 16 inches). The rolling knobs to adjust speed and incline are nicer to use. My partner, who designs commercial and residential interior spaces, agrees with me that the Tread Flex is a better-looking machine.

List price for the Tread Flex is $300 cheaper, but the NordicTrack seems to be perpetually on sale. So it might come down to looks, that 3% decline, or what class platform you'd like to buy into.

After last week’s midterm elections saw them lose at least seven Senate seats and the majority, some Republicans are pushing for a reckoning, saying the conference should stop and think about its future.

In a recent development, “After the stunning defeat [we] just can’t continue on business as usual. That kind of defeat demands change,” Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., noted on Monday evening.

Asked if he himself would want to run for Senate minority leader, the Wisconsin Republican responded with a question of his own: “That’s part of our problem. Who’d want the job? Would you want it?”.

Though no hopeful had emerged as of Monday afternoon — at least publicly — to challenge current Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., for the top GOP post, the frustration was palpable as Republican senators returned to D.C. and grappled with the election results. Calls grew throughout the day to delay the conference’s leadership elections planned for Tuesday morning.

“Well, I mean, I’m open to hearing what the arguments are for that,” Thune told reporters Monday when asked about the possibility of postponing the leadership votes. “I don’t know if that solves anything, but like I said, it’s going to be a decision that’s ultimately made by Republican senators. We’ll hear them out.”.

Recent findings suggest that johnson told reporters on Monday that if the election is held, he would “leave the room” and walk out. Either way, he seemed certain to at least get a “fulsome” discussion of the topic, as he requested in a letter he sent to Republican Conference Chair Tom Cotton, R-Ark. Four other Republican senators signed on to the letter, hitting the threshold to call a conference meeting under internal GOP rules.

Also signed by Sens. Mike Lee of Utah, Ted Budd of North Carolina, Rick Scott of Florida, and John Kennedy of Louisiana, the letter obtained by CQ Roll Call cites last week’s “stunning defeat” and reads in part: “Holding leadership elections without engaging in a robust discussion and evaluation of how those running for leadership intend to lead would be political malpractice.”.

Kennedy mentioned Monday evening that he was asking to postpone the leadership elections because “we need time to talk to each other.”.

“We’re like a shop owner who’s losing his customers. It’s not the customer’s job to fix that. It’s the shop owner’s job, and I’m not looking for blame-shifting. I’m looking for self-examination,” he said, adding that he wouldn’t consider running for minority leader himself.

In the letter, the group asked that at the time the leadership elections were set to begin, 9 a.m. on Tuesday, they instead “have a fulsome conference discussion and delay holding leadership elections until we all have a chance to hear from leadership candidates as to what type of collaborative conference governing model we should adopt and what our strategy will be to counter the emboldened Democrats.”.

Thune echoed that wording Monday as he spoke to reporters, saying, “I do think that we need to have a very fulsome, robust conversation about where we go from here, and then we’ll see what the consensus of the conference is.”.

According to recent reports, but Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., who serves as chair of the Senate Republican Policy Committee, stated she has seen such requests launched in the past and didn’t think it would do much to affect the ultimate outcome. “I think Sen. Thune will be reelected,” she said.

And several Senate GOP aides stated that they suspected a “robust” conversation wouldn’t do much to delay the aims and that leadership elections were still expected to take place Tuesday. They noted similar efforts from some of those same senators in previous years to sow discord in the ranks.

According to recent reports, that includes Scott, who unsuccessfully challenged Thune in 2024 and then-GOP leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., in 2022. But Scott told Fox News over the weekend, “I don’t want to run again. I’ve run twice.”.

Republicans “failed. We had a horrible night,” Scott stated. “Instead of having an [leadership] election, the first thing you do is you say, ‘OK, what are we going to change? We have to change something.’”.

Lee floated the idea of waiting until after the uncalled Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska are officially resolved.

In a recent development, an online pressure campaign was building in some of the same MAGA corners of the internet that have pushed to pass a sweeping voter ID bill, known as the SAVE America Act, that has stalled in the Senate. On Monday morning, influencer Scott Presler in an X post urged constituents to call their senators while praising the lawmakers who have already pushed for the leadership elections to be postponed. “Where is everyone else?” he wrote.

Sens. Jim Banks of Indiana and Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania also called for a delay, though they did not appear on Johnson’s letter.

Sources indicate that “A week ago, we had the worst election results in decades,” McCormick said in a post on X, calling Tuesday “too soon” to vote for leaders. “I know it’s been practice to go straight to leadership elections in recent years, but we should not rush it.”.

Banks similarly stated Tuesday was “too soon,” posting on social media, “Our conference needs to sit down and have a frank conversation about where we fell short, what we stand for, and what we’re going to do for the working families who sent us here.”.

According to recent reports, one senator speaking out in Thune’s defense was Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, who competed with Thune for the top spot in 2024 but on Monday said the leader isn’t to blame for the midterm results.

“I think the president needs to look in the mirror and look at the flawed candidates that he endorsed, and the kind of environment that we’re in,” remarked Cornyn, who is still smarting from losing his primary to a challenger backed by President Donald Trump.

Cornyn’s loss means he has no say in the coming conference leadership elections. But he said, “I think Thune’s a good man, and did as well as he could against a president and an environment that was pretty hostile.”.

A Latest Azzedine Alaïa Retrospective Goes Beyond the Bandage Dress

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Azzedine Alaïa’s designs may not look so radical now, but almost 50 years ago, he changed the collective tide of fashion.
  • Alaïa’s designs “were completely shocking” to the public at the time, recounts Laura Camerlengo, curator in charge of costume and textile arts at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco.
  • Recent findings suggest that born in 1935 in Tunis, Alaïa first trained as a sculptor, a background evident in his body of work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The bandage dress. The zipper dress. The perforated leather. The jersey hoods. The peplummed chemises. Azzedine Alaïa’s designs may not look so radical now, but almost 50 years ago, he changed the collective tide of fashion. The bandage dress is perhaps the most pervasive bit of his legacy, and it is emblematic of how the late French-Tunisian designer ushered in a fresh body-conscious silhouette in the ’80s, one made possible by technological innovations in materials that sculpted without any rigid, waist-cinching structure.

Alaïa’s designs “were completely shocking” to the public at the time, recounts Laura Camerlengo, curator in charge of costume and textile arts at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. She has spent the past four years developing a latest exhibition titled “Azzedine Alaïa: Sculpting Fashion,” the first major U.S. retrospective dedicated to the work of the famed couturier. It opened November 21.

Recent findings suggest that born in 1935 in Tunis, Alaïa first trained as a sculptor, a background evident in his body of work. In 1956, he decamped to Paris to pursue fashion full-time. After a brief internship at the house of Christian Dior, he worked under Guy Laroche for less than two years before taking on his own private clients, then launching his own atelier in the late ’70s. From there, he built the house we know today. His obsession with construction and material innovation allowed him to both celebrate and liberate the female form. He passed away in late 2017 at the age of 82.

Industry observers note that camerlengo first encountered Alaïa’s work as an assistant on the “Patrick Kelly Runway of Love” exhibition that the Philadelphia Museum of Art organized in 2014. “I was intrigued by how many of the newly introduced designers in Paris at this time were being supported by US consumers and retailers,” she notes. After ascending to her new position in San Francisco years later, she cold-emailed Olivier Saillard, director of the Azzedine Alaïa Foundation in Paris. He was intrigued, and the two began working together on the exhibition almost immediately.

Sources indicate that the exhibition focuses on 80 garments from across Alaïa’s celebrated career, divided over a series of archetypes—the bandage dresses, sculptures and shapes, black and white, silhouettes and suiting, and construction and craftsmanship—to explore how his design aesthetic evolved. Interspersed are designs worn by devotees like Tina Turner, Grace Jones, and Rihanna. One final gallery highlights his personal collections of the work of designers he most admired, like Christian Dior and Charles James.

Ahead, Camerlengo speaks to Bazaar about curating the latest exhibition, contextualizing Alaïa’s work in today’s fashion landscape, and his enduring legacy.

Recent findings suggest that the exhibition is not chronological. We look at a series of Alaïa’s archetypes like the bandage dress to explore how his design aesthetic evolved over the course of his career. He often himself mentioned that he didn’t want to conform to seasonal trends; he was more interested in the evolution of his designs. And so the gallery shows a mix of objects dating from the 1980s to his final collection in 2017, and they’re largely grouped by type.

In a recent development, when you come in, you are greeted by Grace Jones, as we say, and the seminal purple hooded bandage dress from the fashion Oscars [a French event held in 1985]. As you move through, you’ll see a selection of the zipper dresses, the chiffon gowns, and other works that tie into some of the other themes. In each space, we mix the time periods. And that was something Alaïa himself often remarked. [He had a running joke that he didn’t know his own age.] He often said he was “as old as the pharaohs.” Basically, time was a construct for him.

That’s a great word for it. We could think of the popularity of the Japanese fashion designers who obscured women’s bodies with their voluminous styles. We could think of the suiting of the period. The 1970s is this period of workplace equality. Women are wearing suits in the style of masculine dress, but that also means they're obscuring their bodies. And then we can think of pop culture. I always think of Diane Keaton’s Annie Hall in 1977.

In a recent development, some of the individuals I interviewed for my catalog text who were retailers in San Francisco at the time described Alaïa's designs as being like a whiplash. It was a complete 180 from the styles that they had gotten used to over the past decade, which also includes the rise of T-shirts and jeans for women as a mode of dress.

In a recent development, so here you have these very sexy, very form-fitting clothes. And part of the Alaïa aesthetic, as I see it, is the reclamation of the gaze. Rather than women being passively looked at—usually by men—they are instead commanding their own agency. As you remarked, it was completely earth-shattering and very shocking at the time.

Azzedine Alaïa was one of the few couturiers who could work completely by the methods of tailoring and by draping, start to finish, from the initial concept to the final product. I did not fully appreciate his tailoring and the suits he constructed beforehand. We have a selection of them in a gallery of the exhibition, and their construction is absolutely incredible. The way they fit the body, the way they uplift and empower women through cloth—again, very antithetical to what we saw in the decades prior in the 1970s. These are very form-fitting, tailored at the waist, but they have soft feminine touches as well that give you this interesting mix of femininity and strength at the same time.

Industry observers note that very crucial. We talk in the first gallery about how women, speaking generally, were the architects of his life. He learned to sew from his sister, who was working for a seamstress. He was encouraged by a local midwife in Tunisia to go to school at the Institute of Fine Arts. She helped him forge his papers to read 16—he was only 15 at the time. He learned his skills, not in formal training, but from women in Tunisia.

And then his early work was supported by a lot of leading figures of international society, including various Rothschilds, the French performer Arletty, the Swedish American actress Greta Garbo, and that's all before he even started to work formally under his own label in the 1980s. Of course, in the 1980s, he adopts Naomi Campbell, who becomes his protégé. He has close relationships with Grace Jones and Tina Turner. They were hugely notable to him. In the exhibition, the clear invisible mounts that we use are actually based on the body of Naomi Campbell.

Probably the Grace Jones bandage dress from the fashion Oscars in 1985. Not only is it the progression of the bandage dress style that he experiments with throughout the course of the 1980s, but it represents a key moment in his career where he receives two very high accolades as part of the fashion Oscars and he’s recognized for his genius.

As far as the designs themselves, I think we would consider the bandage dress, for example, an iconic symbol of late 20th- and 21st-century fashion developed by Azzedine Alaïa, but of course iterated upon extensively. We've seen surges and resurgences in its popularity ever since.

And then as far as the landscape of the broader fashion system, Alaïa was someone who really eschewed seasonal calendars and trends. He was unconcerned with making things for the market. He often wanted to just produce clothes and share them when he felt they were ready. So I think his method of working foreshadows some of the conversations we’re having now about the overproduction of fashion and the overconsumption of fashion, even the detrimental environmental impacts that we see connected to it. He was really a forerunner, in a sense, to question the fashion system.

Recent findings suggest that you can see how he really studied the construction of other garments and then adapted it in his own way in his designs. For example, he admired the work of Charles James, the great American fashion designer who was able to manipulate fabric to achieve weightless volume. And you see in Alaïa's own collections as he continues in his career, he does radial tucks and pleating to also get a certain amount of weightless volume in some of his gowns, very much in the spirit of James.

Recent findings suggest that I hope our visitors appreciate the artistry of his work, first and foremost, and also the importance of handcraftsmanship. We are increasingly in an age of technology, especially with the rise of AI. What he created by his own hand is something that we can really marvel at.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It started, as things often do for Kevin Zak, as an idea for a meme.

Recent findings suggest that the playwright behind last year’s Ginger Twinsies, a Millennial satire of The Parent Trap, is more widely known for his presence on social media, where his pop culture memes sit right at the corner of Extremely Online and Incredibly Gay. (This likely had something to do, he admits, with growing up with two gay brothers and a father who would decorate their front door with a giant Academy Award cutout on Oscars night.).

A Kidman Carol, his latest play, stemmed from his idea for a spin on the Dickens classic in which Cate Blanchett is visited by Nicole Kidman in order to learn the true meaning of awards season. When a friend who runs the Alleyway Theatre in Buffalo, Newly introduced York, offered a few nights to workshop anything he wanted in 2024, Zak knew just the holiday program he wanted to see.

Enter Marla Mindelle and Josh Sharp, who now play Kidman and Blanchett in the show’s off-Broadway premiere. As Mindelle puts it, “The world of theater is so small, off-Broadway even smaller, and alt queer comedy is literally a basement limited to about 10 people, and we are three out of those 10.” She has a point: Mindelle’s massively popular Titanique and Sharp’s A24-backed film Dicks: The Musical both started at (literally) underground comedy clubs.

Recent findings suggest that when Zak asked them if they’d like to participate in a workshop presentation that took place last winter, Mindelle notes she and Sharp texted on the side: “I’ll do it if you do it. It’s five performances. What can go wrong?”.

Sharp and Richard Perez in A Kidman Carol.

“And what can go wrong is a full six-week run at the off-Broadway mall,” Sharp quips, referencing the curious, five-theater layout of Upcoming World Stages.

Just in time for the holidays, and with awards season just around the corner, Vogue caught up with the comedy trio to discuss Kidman and Blanchett’s unending star power.

Vogue: Was there ever a question as to which stars you wanted to feature in the show?

Kevin Zak: It was always centered around them.

Sources indicate that josh Sharp: They sort of exemplify this distinction really well, where Cate is more of a “pure actress” who’s like, “Why do I have to make TikToks? I want to act.” And, in the show, we get into how Nicole has leveraged some of that power to be like, “Because I’m a celebrity, I can make all this stuff.” I think because Cate is a person that people know less [about]—you don’t really have a Cate Blanchett impression—she feels a little more like everywoman, and it means we can bend her into being Scrooge. She’s mostly known for her intensity, so she can become a good stand-in for a curmudgeon who wishes the state of the world were different, and Nicole can agree but be a bit more hopeful about it. How do they change each other?

Industry observers note that zak: Besides being all lesbians that have mental breakdowns, Cate’s characters all have the energy of, The world is against me, everyone is trying to get me, like in Tár or Carol or Notes on a Scandal. That feels like a good engine for her throughout the show: As curmudgeonly as she comes across, she’s trying to open your eyes to what the hell is going on, and is anyone going to do anything about it?

Recent findings suggest that this is a very earnestly pro-awards show play. What was the last shockingly good Oscar win?

Marla Mindelle: What if I remarked Adrian Brody’s second Oscar?

Industry observers note that sharp: What if I said Green Book? There’s gotta be one past this, but my gut goes with Moonlight winning best picture. That was such an affirming culture-stopper to me, where I was like, Thank God we’re allowing movies like that, with zero dollars, to actually win.

It has been revealed that zak: Minari, when Youn Yuh-jung won [for best supporting actress]. Brad Pitt was a producer of the movie and she scolded him for never coming to set during her acceptance speech.

Marla, what have you discovered in your Nicole deep dive?

It has been revealed that mindelle: I rewatched To Die For, which I think actually might be my favorite Nicole Kidman film, even over Moulin Rouge!, which I can’t believe I’m saying because Moulin Rouge! was also my sexual awakening. Compared to Cate, I feel like Nicole has 10% more camp. Nicole knows what she is serving and has a little wink about it, like “I know I’m so beautiful and so talented,” where Cate is: “Yes, and I’m also all about the work.”.

It has been revealed that zak: What makes them different in their performances, at least for me, is that Nicole’s characters get hurt and Cate’s characters get mad. In Substantial Little Lies, you see this woman in this horrible relationship get hurt, even in her therapy sessions. Even when her therapist is so bluntly truthful with her, all she can really say is, “I think you’re way out of line,” which is a line in our show. Cate is on the defensive. I feel that hurt is disguised with rage, a lot of the time. But that’s what really draws me to them, that core emotional difference. And they’ve never done a movie together, which is so crazy.

When did you each realize Nicole was a star?

Sharp: It was probably Batman Forever.

Sources indicate that zak: Definitely Dr. Chase Meridian in Batman Forever.

Recent findings suggest that mindelle: I remember her having sex in To Die For. That was a pivotal moment where I was like, Oh my God, what is this feeling so sudden and newly introduced inside my body? I re-watched it recently and it really is one of the greatest movies ever. She is phenomenal.

According to recent reports, zak: That makes sense. [It’s] why you play her so horny.

Recent findings suggest that mindelle: It’s not even horny. I just feel like she’s always, like, loose and up for anything.

Mindelle: If you offered her poppers at The Eagle, she’d be like, “Why not?” She’ll do it.

Sources indicate that sharp: I’ve loved The Talented Mr. Ripley since I was young, but I really think Tár is one of the greatest films of the decade. I saw it four times in theaters. I heard people go, “Isn’t it sort of so long and slow and boring?” I’m like, Absolutely, let’s go!

According to recent reports, zak: Notes on a Scandal. I remember going to see it for Judi Dench and then being served Cate Blanchett having a mental breakdown in that press sequence, with her black eyeliner running as she’s just moan-screaming to be left alone. I finally saw myself onscreen.

In writing and preparing for this, were you trying to get into what these women are actually like, or was it all based on their public perception?

Industry observers note that zak: There is a combo of both. Cate, especially, her version of Scrooge is not someone we disagree with, like we do in A Christmas Carol. She makes solid points about the state of, not only the industry, but the planet. She’s been very vocal about her opinions. Her foundation is an anti-AI foundation and, on Las Culturistas, she spoke about how much award season has gotten overblown and how it should be a private event, if we’re going to do it at all. And then, of course, there’s her tirade on leaf blowers and how much she hates them. And then Nicole is truly up for anything, but she also uplifts people. She’s spoken a lot about how she uses her name to uplift young female screenwriters, young female directors, and putting her name on projects so that they get greenlit.

Marla, how’d you develop your insanely good Kidman impression?

Mindelle: The great thing about doing a role like this—a minimal, meaty role like this—is that it’s made me watch a lot of old Nicole Kidman movies. I feel like a kid again because I’m watching all these incredibly nostalgic movies from the ’80s, ’90s, and realizing her body of work is absolutely incredible. And whatever she has become now is almost this camp amalgamation of the past 30 to 40 years of her work. We’re just living in her timeline.

Zak: It feels like there’s never been a dip for Nicole, in terms of movie stardom. She’s only continued to rise in likability, popularity, talent, star power. There was never an era where you thought, Where’d Nicole Kidman go? And on top of being an incredible actress and movie star, she’s now a fashion icon and clubbing in Ibiza, and things like that. She seems like this ethereal presence on earth, which I think gives way for her to be the representation of cinema as ghosts in this show.

Do you have a personal favorite line?

Sharp: “I am Petra’s father” [from Tár].

Recent findings suggest that mindelle: For me, it’s “That indescribable feeling” [from Kidman’s AMC pre-show ad]. There’s something about her “indescribable” that helped me tap into Nicole.

The Best Pregnancy-Safe Sunscreens, According to a Dermatologist

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (720 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elle

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor.
  • According to recent reports, pregnancy often requires an overhaul of your skin care routine—mainly due to ingredients not being tested for safety during pregnancy and because hormonal shifts can cause skin changes that require a new set of products.
  • Recent findings suggest that during pregnancy, Olamiju recommends mineral-based sunscreens as the first choice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

According to recent reports, pregnancy often requires an overhaul of your skin care routine—mainly due to ingredients not being tested for safety during pregnancy and because hormonal shifts can cause skin changes that require a new set of products. One non-negotiable in any daily skin care line is sunscreen. Although the choice between chemical SPF and a mineral one is usually a personal preference, several considerations should be made during pregnancy, under the guidance of a medical professional. Dr. Brianna Olamiju, a board-certified dermatologist with Spring Street Dermatology in NYC, explains to ELLE which are the safest sunscreen formulas to use during pregnancy and which ingredients to avoid.

Recent findings suggest that during pregnancy, Olamiju recommends mineral-based sunscreens as the first choice. Look for formulations with zinc oxide, titanium dioxide, or a combination of both. “Mineral sunscreens work by forming a protective layer on the skin and are particularly appealing during pregnancy because their active ingredients have minimal absorption through the skin,” she explains. They also tend to be well tolerated by individuals with sensitive skin, which can become more reactive during pregnancy.

Recent findings suggest that some of Olamiju’s top picks are EltaMD UV Physical Broad-Spectrum SPF 41, La Roche-Posay Anthelios Mineral Tinted Sunscreen SPF 50, CeraVe Hydrating Mineral Sunscreen SPF 50, and Blue Lizard Sensitive Mineral Sunscreen SPF 50. “For patients experiencing melasma or pregnancy-related hyperpigmentation, I particularly like tinted mineral sunscreens containing iron oxides, as these provide additional protection against visible light, which can contribute to worsening pigmentation,” says Olamiju. Ultimately, she adds, the best sunscreen is one that feels comfortable on the skin and that you’ll want to use consistently.

Sources indicate that according to Olamiju, there’s right now limited research specifically evaluating the safety of chemical sunscreen ingredients during pregnancy. However, she notes this does not mean all chemical sunscreens have been proven unsafe. “Some chemical sunscreen ingredients can be absorbed through the skin and detected in the bloodstream, but systemic absorption alone does not establish that an ingredient causes harm to a developing baby,” she explains. At this time, there is insufficient evidence to conclude that using chemical sunscreen as directed causes adverse pregnancy outcomes.

Recent findings suggest that that stated, as a precautionary approach, she recommends choosing mineral-based sunscreens containing zinc oxide and titanium dioxide during pregnancy. “It is key to emphasize that patients should not avoid sunscreen altogether out of concern about chemical ingredients, as protecting the skin from ultraviolet radiation remains extremely important during pregnancy.”.

The sun protection factor (SPF) is crucial during pregnancy, just as it is any other time. Olamiju explains that pregnancy can increase the likelihood of developing hyperpigmentation, particularly melasma, commonly referred to as the pregnancy mask. “Hormonal changes can stimulate melanin production, making the skin more susceptible to discoloration, especially with sun exposure.” To get ahead of it, she recommends using a broad-spectrum sunscreen with an SPF of at least 30, although she adds that an SPF 50 is an excellent option for those who spend significant time outdoors or are particularly prone to pigmentation.

As a precaution, Olamiju recommends avoiding sunscreen formulations containing oxybenzone and octinoxate when practical, given research concerns raised about their potential endocrine-disrupting properties and the limited pregnancy-specific safety data. Beyond sunscreen filters, she indicates to also be mindful of other active ingredients like retinoids, including retinol, tretinoin, and adapalene, which should be avoided during pregnancy, as should hydroquinone. “When in doubt, patients should review their skincare regimen with their dermatologist and obstetrician.”.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to a mineral-based formula with zinc oxide, titanium dioxide, or both, and an SPF of 30 or higher, Olamiju also recommends a water-resistant sunscreen, particularly if you exercise outdoors, swim, or spend extended periods in the sun. For anyone experiencing melasma or increased pigmentation during pregnancy, she also says to consider a tinted mineral sunscreen containing iron oxides to provide additional protection against visible light. If you have sensitive or pregnancy-related reactive skin, you may also benefit from fragrance-free, noncomedogenic formulations. “I generally prefer lotions, creams, or sunscreen sticks over sprays to ensure adequate application and minimize the risk of inhaling airborne particles,” Olamiju adds.

You’ll be able to tell a lot about your date by their reaction to this idea and how they carry themselves throughout the volunteering.

This one will really test your teamwork. You can either grab a premade kit or go old-school and use a pint-sized milk carton and graham crackers as your base. Grab marshmallows of all sizes, candy canes, whipped cream (I personally love the boozy vodka-infused peppermint one from Whipshots), and whatever else sounds enticing. In a recent development, karaoke isn’t about who sounds the best but who has the best energy. Belt out your favorite holiday jams, from the classics to latest renditions of the season’s most popular songs. It’s truly a perfect way to bond and see if your date can match your vibe.

This option is such a fun way to spend time together. In a recent development, the best way to spread holiday cheer is by supporting local businesses.
