#215139. The 7 Lessons I Learned About Skin After Losing 85 Pounds

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1433 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Harpersbazaar ↗ Open Full Page

The 7 Lessons I Learned About Skin After Losing 85 Pounds

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1433 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Harpersbazaar

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that I lost 85 pounds without bariatric surgery.
  • In a recent development, because I’m losing weight more slowly, I haven’t yet encountered loose skin, though I still have at least 50 more pounds to go.
  • It has been revealed that it’s a pretty unsexy topic—which is why it’s rarely, if ever, discussed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I lost 85 pounds without bariatric surgery. Weight loss has been on my mind basically my entire life, especially since I started this journey in earnest in July 2019. And, as proud of myself as I most certainly am for losing this weight and finally getting healthier, it is met toe-to-toe with pervasive anxiety and a nagging question: What about excess skin?

In a recent development, because I’m losing weight more slowly, I haven’t yet encountered loose skin, though I still have at least 50 more pounds to go. I worry, perhaps too much, about whether I’ll make it to my goal weight without needing skin tightening at the end of this journey.

It has been revealed that it’s a pretty unsexy topic—which is why it’s rarely, if ever, discussed. But for those like me who are on major weight-loss journeys, or whose bodies have changed significantly through pregnancy, it’s a question that plagues us: Am I going to encounter excess skin the more weight I lose? And if I do, what can I do about it?

Apparently, I’m not the only one with questions, according to New York City plastic surgeon Lara Devgan. “Skin tightening remains one of the elusive black boxes in the world of plastic surgery,” she indicates. That said, we’re all still learning about best practices—from me to medical professionals.

So I decided to dig deeper. I rounded up five renowned dermatologists and plastic surgeons from across the country and asked them my questions. And here’s what they have to say.

It has been revealed that “Losing weight gradually rather than rapidly may prevent excess skin after major weight loss,” claims Los Angeles–based dermatologist Harold Lancer. “However, rapid large-scale weight loss will invariably result in excess skin.” Devgan seconds that. “The best way to prevent skin laxity after weight loss is to do your best to lose weight at a slow and steady pace,” she says. “Although it may sound appealing to get to the finish line quickly, that is actually the worst thing you can do in terms of skin laxity.” Losing weight slowly, she says, allows the skin to contract and shrink as the body shape changes.

Industry observers note that though I personally haven’t opted for weight loss surgery, many do—and there is zero shame in that. But because weight is lost more rapidly after surgery, the likelihood of excess skin increases, so experts recommend pairing weight loss surgery with a skin removal procedure. Why worry about excess skin, especially after faster weight loss? It’s “because collagen and elastin fibers are destroyed when skin is stretched significantly and remains stretched for an extended amount of time,” says New York City plastic surgeon David Shafer. “Patients should blueprint on staged procedures if having a weight loss surgery followed by a skin removal surgery.”.

“Typically, younger patients with thicker and more sebaceous skin will have more skin contraction during weight loss due to better elasticity,” Devgan states. “Starting in the 20s, tissue elasticity begins to decline. Even in the absence of weight fluctuation, loss of tissue turgor and decreased firmness can be seen in midface descent in the late 20s, breast laxity in the 30s, abdominal laxity in the 40s, and extremity laxity in the 50s.”.

However, Devgan claims everyone’s body is different. “There is a tremendous amount of variability in the human experience, so some patients may lose 50 pounds with minimal change in their body, while others can lose as few as 10 and see tissue laxity.” If you are genetically blessed with unusually superb tissue elasticity, Devgan says, it can be less dramatic. (And lucky you.).

Lifestyle choices can also factor in, Boston-based dermatologist Ranella Hirsch says. How long were you at the weight you started losing from? Are you a smoker? Do you spend a lot of time in the sun without protection? All these factors play into skin elasticity.

“Using an emollient moisturizer rich in vitamin E will help improve the barrier protection of the skin and lock in moisture,” Devgan says. She also says the topical medical-grade ingredients you use on your face for firmness and tightness—like hyaluronic acid, peptides, niacin, squalene, vitamins C and B, retinol, and bakuchiol—can work elsewhere, too. “Most people focus on using these for the face and neck in their daily routines, but from a molecular perspective, their efficacy is present anywhere on the body.” But save your money on creams that promise you the world. “Losing large amounts of weight rapidly tends to leave skin behind,” Hirsch says. “Though creams with incredible claims abound, they actually do little.”.

Nécessaire The Body Lotion with Niacinamide.

Biossance Squalane + Caffeine Toning Body Cream.

Sol de Janeiro Bom Dia Bright Body Cream with Vitamin C.

Augustinus Bader The Body Cream.

U Beauty The SCULPT Arm Compound Body Serum.

Industry observers note that building muscle through weight training might help reduce the appearance of lax skin, Upcoming York City dermatologist Dendy Engelman states. “This helps reduce the appearance by replacing the lost fat with muscle mass.”.

Nonsurgical options can help with loose skin after weight loss, but they won’t help with skin folds or hanging skin. “Noninvasive treatments such as laser and radiofrequency can help tighten the skin, but there is a limit to how much they can do,” Shafer adds. “Hanging skin generally needs to be surgically excised with procedures such as abdominoplasty, body lift, and arm lift.” Shafer notes there’s a difference between loose skin and hanging skin. “It’s possible patients can manage and treat excess skin cases without undergoing skin removal surgery, such as if the skin is loose but not hanging.” He adds, “In that case, noninvasive treatments may be useful, but hanging skin most often requires surgical excision.”.

“After major weight loss, people may have skin that hangs off their body,” Engelman says. “These heavy folds can cause health problems such as pain, inflammation, and frequent infections from the skin constantly rubbing together. This can happen during exercise or everyday activities. When a person is having functional complications because of their excess skin, it should be a sign that this problem needs to be addressed.” And, of course, everyone’s journey is different.

Recent findings suggest that lancer notes some individuals will tolerate moderate laxity and be happy with the weight-loss accomplishment; others will seek skin tightening for as little as a five-pound weight loss. But, he says, if plastic surgery does become the option on the table, “I would recommend getting at least three opinions from doctors who exclusively do excess body skin reduction. Once you select a doctor, do one small area on your body, so you can evaluate the procedure, how your body heals, and your results. Afterward, you can determine whether you’d like to proceed with a full-blown larger procedure.”.

Industry observers note that he suggests consulting a dermatologist for nonsurgical options, then asking that doctor to recommend plastic surgeons who specialize in excess body skin reduction if you feel that is the right path for you. This is a major decision and shouldn’t be taken lightly. Bring medical professionals along for the entire weight-loss journey (even if you’ve already started) and ask all the questions: Which specific procedure is best? How much will it cost? Will insurance cover it? (From my research so far, no, if it is cosmetic, but perhaps yes if it would help correct something that limits your daily functionality.) No question is off-limits, and don’t try to make these decisions alone.

If this piece applies to you at all, whether it’s longstanding weight you carried, weight you lost during pregnancy, or somewhere in between, that means one thing: You’ve taken major steps toward better physical health, and that should be applauded. “Everyone’s weight loss story is different, and some days are harder than others,” Engelman says. “I say, try to be kind to yourself. You’ve just reached a huge accomplishment and should be proud of that.”.

It has been revealed that devgan agrees. “Accomplishing a personal health goal like major weight loss is an incredible achievement that anyone should be proud of,” she says. “While excess skin can feel like a burden or source of self-consciousness, it is also a reminder of the metaphorical and literal shedding of the weight of a prior version of oneself. You cannot have a couture gown without a seam, and you cannot have a surgery without a scar. Life has limitations, but that does not make it less beautiful. It makes it more real.”.

Should You Worry About That Bump on Your Chest?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (841 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’re like most guys, you probably have plenty of little bumps and lumps on your skin.
  • While male breast cancer is rare, estimates suggest that more than 2,600 men are diagnosed with an invasive form of the disease each year in the United States, and more than 500 die, according to the American Cancer Society.
  • There isn’t a universal description of what breast cancer lumps look like in men, but there are some common characteristics to keep in mind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’re like most guys, you probably have plenty of little bumps and lumps on your skin. There’s the callus on your toe from training for that 10K, the razor bumps along your neck from this morning’s shave, and the skin tag on your underarm you keep meaning to get removed. While it’s often completely fine to ignore these bumps, that isn’t always the case. Some can be a red flag worth paying attention to—especially if they’re on your chest.

While male breast cancer is rare, estimates suggest that more than 2,600 men are diagnosed with an invasive form of the disease each year in the United States, and more than 500 die, according to the American Cancer Society. And one of its telltale signs is a firm bump under or near your nipple. Below, find out more about what a breast-cancer lump may look like and four other things that could be to blame for a upcoming bump on your chest.

There isn’t a universal description of what breast cancer lumps look like in men, but there are some common characteristics to keep in mind. “Breast cancer in men typically presents as a painless, firm, or hard lump,” says Jose Pablo Leone, MD, the director of the Program for Breast Cancer in Men at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston.

According to recent reports, another sign that the bump could be breast cancer is if it’s behind or very close to the nipple and areola. “Men have much less developed breast glandular tissue than women, which is why breast cancer in men most commonly develops near or behind the nipple,” says Dr. Leone. As for size even a lump as small as a pea can be cancerous, but by the time men go to the doctor, tumors are often larger than a marble, according to Dr. Leone. “In part because of the lack of awareness and screening, most men present with larger tumors,” he says. “But any size is worth mentioning to your doctor. Not all breast cancers feel the same, so any upcoming or persistent breast lump should be evaluated by a healthcare professional.”.

Your chest has a lot of oil glands, which can set the stage for pimples. “Staying in a sweaty shirt after a workout can make chest acne flare, especially if the fabric is tight and rubs against your skin,” notes Elizabeth Bahar Houshmand, MD, a board-certified dermatologist based in Dallas. While blackheads and whiteheads are typically small and easy to identify, inflamed pimples or nodules may seem more alarming because they can be hard, painful, and form deep under the skin. When it comes to nodular acne specifically, you can’t treat it on your own. If that’s what you think you’re dealing with, see a dermatologist, who can prescribe an oral or topical medication to help clear it up.

In a recent development, “This is a collection of fat that forms under the skin,” says Sonya Kenkare, MD, a board-certified dermatologist at Illinois Dermatology Institute in Hinsdale, Illinois. “It is usually soft, not painful, and you can move it around in all different directions.” You don’t need to do anything about a lipoma, but if you want to get it removed, you can talk to a doctor about it.

In a recent development, when hair follicles get inflamed or infected, you can end up with folliculitis. “Folliculitis often looks like small pimples or pus-filled bumps centered around a hair follicle” indicates Dr. Houshmand. “They may itch or feel tender.”.

According to recent reports, blockage or damage to a hair follicle can also cause epidermal inclusion cysts. These cysts occur when dead skin cells get trapped under the surface instead of shedding. “They feel somewhat firm and often have a central little black spot,” indicates Dr. Kenkare. Sometimes simply applying a warm compress to the area can help a cyst heal on its own, but a doctor can also inject it with a steroid to reduce swelling, drain it, or surgically remove it.

According to recent reports, this condition occurs when breast tissue gets enlarged in men, and it can first appear as a lump under your nipple. “It often feels like a rubbery or firm disc beneath the nipple, and it may be tender,” indicates Dr. Houshmand. While gynecomastia can come on as a side effect of some medications, like antibiotics or antidepressants, or diseases like thyroid disorders, sometimes there is no clear cause at all.

Sources indicate that if you’re starting to feel like it’s difficult to tell on your own what the lump on your chest might be, you’re not wrong. That’s why it’s best to have your primary care physician look at any upcoming, unexplained bumps and tell you whether you need imaging, like a mammogram with an ultrasound. That may sound scary, but it’s really just covering your bases. “Uncommon things are uncommon, and breast cancer in men is uncommon,” states Dr. Leone. “You shouldn’t worry excessively about male breast cancer, but you should be aware of it.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A group of incoming members of Congress and staff arrive on Capitol Hill for new member orientation on Monday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

What happens when more than 100 members-elect descend on Capitol Hill a week after Election Day?

As Rep.-elect Dan Koh, D-Mass., put it, “It really is like high school — but it’s fun high school.”.

Trainings and guest speakers aren’t everyone’s idea of a fun time, but Democrats are feeling good about this year’s fresh member orientation. Giddy, even.

It has been revealed that the incoming freshmen will pose for a class photo on the House steps. They’ll test their luck in a lottery to see who lands the best office space. And everywhere they look, they see signs of the blue wave that swept over the country.

“I think — well, I hope — that we will be doing a lot of exceeding expectations in this caucus. The American people deserve it and expect it,” stated Rep.-elect Sam Forstag, D-Mont., as he headed to lunch after an orientation session on Monday.

Recent findings suggest that forstag is the first Democratic congressman from Montana in 30 years, succeeding retiring GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke. A former smokejumper who parachuted into remote forests to put out wildfires, Forstag won by more than 3 points in a district President Donald Trump carried by double digits in 2024.

The 120th Congress will be full of history-makers, and a record-breaking number of women are set to serve in the House.

The math isn’t lost on Republicans navigating a freshman class where they have fewer peers than they hoped.

In a recent development, “I thought that it would probably go a little bit different. I think a lot of people did, but it is what it is. You work with what we have,” said Rep.-elect Mark Lamb, R-Ariz.

In a recent development, but just like high school, everyone’s trying to make friends. As incoming members filed into the Capitol Visitor Center on Monday morning, Rep.-elect Cait Conley, D-N.Y., introduced herself to Rep.-elect Sydney Gruters, R-Fla.

Meanwhile, Rep.-elect Claire Valdez, D-N.Y., who describes herself as a “proud democratic socialist,” walked by chatting with Del.-elect Robert White, who will become only the third person in the modern era to hold the title of D.C.’s nonvoting delegate.

Rep.-elect Brad Lander, D-N.Y., who ousted fellow Democrat Dan Goldman in a Brooklyn-based primary before cruising to victory in the general election, was also making friends.

“It’s obviously a lot different when it’s you,” he said.

Koh agreed, saying “everyone in that room, Republican or Democrat, had a lot of reverence for where they were.”.

“I think it was just a good reminder about how despite all the division, that’s what we’re going to focus on — trying to figure out how to get things done for the American people,” he remarked.

I Lost 85 Pounds. What Happens to My Skin Now?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1444 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Harpersbazaar

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that I lost 85 pounds without bariatric surgery.
  • Sources indicate that because I’m losing weight more slowly, I haven’t yet encountered loose skin, though I still have at least 50 more pounds to go.
  • According to recent reports, it’s a pretty unsexy topic—which is why it’s rarely, if ever, discussed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I lost 85 pounds without bariatric surgery. Weight loss has been on my mind basically my entire life, especially since I started this journey in earnest in July 2019. And, as proud of myself as I most certainly am for losing this weight and finally getting healthier, it is met toe-to-toe with pervasive anxiety and a nagging question: What about excess skin?

Sources indicate that because I’m losing weight more slowly, I haven’t yet encountered loose skin, though I still have at least 50 more pounds to go. I worry, perhaps too much, about whether I’ll make it to my goal weight without needing skin tightening at the end of this journey.

According to recent reports, it’s a pretty unsexy topic—which is why it’s rarely, if ever, discussed. But for those like me who are on major weight-loss journeys, or whose bodies have changed significantly through pregnancy, it’s a question that plagues us: Am I going to encounter excess skin the more weight I lose? And if I do, what can I do about it?

Sources indicate that apparently, I’m not the only one with questions, according to New York City plastic surgeon Lara Devgan. “Skin tightening remains one of the elusive black boxes in the world of plastic surgery,” she claims. That noted, we’re all still learning about best practices—from me to medical professionals.

Recent findings suggest that so I decided to dig deeper. I rounded up five renowned dermatologists and plastic surgeons from across the country and asked them my questions. And here’s what they have to say.

It has been revealed that “Losing weight gradually rather than rapidly may prevent excess skin after major weight loss,” notes Los Angeles–based dermatologist Harold Lancer. “However, rapid large-scale weight loss will invariably result in excess skin.” Devgan seconds that. “The best way to prevent skin laxity after weight loss is to do your best to lose weight at a slow and steady pace,” she says. “Although it may sound appealing to get to the finish line rapidly, that is actually the worst thing you can do in terms of skin laxity.” Losing weight slowly, she says, allows the skin to contract and shrink as the body shape changes.

In a recent development, though I personally haven’t opted for weight loss surgery, many do—and there is zero shame in that. But because weight is lost more rapidly after surgery, the likelihood of excess skin increases, so experts recommend pairing weight loss surgery with a skin removal procedure. Why worry about excess skin, especially after faster weight loss? It’s “because collagen and elastin fibers are destroyed when skin is stretched significantly and remains stretched for an extended amount of time,” states Newly introduced York City plastic surgeon David Shafer. “Patients should strategy on staged procedures if having a weight loss surgery followed by a skin removal surgery.”.

“Typically, younger patients with thicker and more sebaceous skin will have more skin contraction during weight loss due to better elasticity,” Devgan says. “Starting in the 20s, tissue elasticity begins to decline. Even in the absence of weight fluctuation, loss of tissue turgor and decreased firmness can be seen in midface descent in the late 20s, breast laxity in the 30s, abdominal laxity in the 40s, and extremity laxity in the 50s.”.

Industry observers note that however, Devgan states everyone’s body is different. “There is a tremendous amount of variability in the human experience, so some patients may lose 50 pounds with minimal change in their body, while others can lose as few as 10 and see tissue laxity.” If you are genetically blessed with unusually superb tissue elasticity, Devgan says, it can be less dramatic. (And lucky you.).

Recent findings suggest that lifestyle choices can also factor in, Boston-based dermatologist Ranella Hirsch says. How long were you at the weight you started losing from? Are you a smoker? Do you spend a lot of time in the sun without protection? All these factors play into skin elasticity.

“Using an emollient moisturizer rich in vitamin E will help improve the barrier protection of the skin and lock in moisture,” Devgan says. She also says the topical medical-grade ingredients you use on your face for firmness and tightness—like hyaluronic acid, peptides, niacin, squalene, vitamins C and B, retinol, and bakuchiol—can work elsewhere, too. “Most people focus on using these for the face and neck in their daily routines, but from a molecular perspective, their efficacy is present anywhere on the body.” But save your money on creams that promise you the world. “Losing large amounts of weight rapidly tends to leave skin behind,” Hirsch says. “Though creams with incredible claims abound, they actually do little.”.

Nécessaire The Body Lotion with Niacinamide.

Biossance Squalane + Caffeine Toning Body Cream.

Sol de Janeiro Bom Dia Bright Body Cream with Vitamin C.

Augustinus Bader The Body Cream.

U Beauty The SCULPT Arm Compound Body Serum.

Industry observers note that building muscle through weight training might help reduce the appearance of lax skin, Newly introduced York City dermatologist Dendy Engelman notes. “This helps reduce the appearance by replacing the lost fat with muscle mass.”.

Nonsurgical options can help with loose skin after weight loss, but they won’t help with skin folds or hanging skin. “Noninvasive treatments such as laser and radiofrequency can help tighten the skin, but there is a limit to how much they can do,” Shafer adds. “Hanging skin generally needs to be surgically excised with procedures such as abdominoplasty, body lift, and arm lift.” Shafer says there’s a difference between loose skin and hanging skin. “It’s possible patients can manage and treat excess skin cases without undergoing skin removal surgery, such as if the skin is loose but not hanging.” He adds, “In that case, noninvasive treatments may be useful, but hanging skin most often requires surgical excision.”.

“After major weight loss, people may have skin that hangs off their body,” Engelman states. “These heavy folds can cause health problems such as pain, inflammation, and frequent infections from the skin constantly rubbing together. This can happen during exercise or everyday activities. When a person is having functional issues because of their excess skin, it should be a sign that this problem needs to be addressed.” And, of course, everyone’s journey is different.

Lancer claims some individuals will tolerate moderate laxity and be happy with the weight-loss accomplishment; others will seek skin tightening for as little as a five-pound weight loss. But, he says, if plastic surgery does become the option on the table, “I would recommend getting at least three opinions from doctors who exclusively do excess body skin reduction. Once you select a doctor, do one small area on your body, so you can evaluate the procedure, how your body heals, and your results. Afterward, you can determine whether you’d like to proceed with a full-blown larger procedure.”.

Recent findings suggest that he suggests consulting a dermatologist for nonsurgical options, then asking that doctor to recommend plastic surgeons who specialize in excess body skin reduction if you feel that is the right path for you. This is a major decision and shouldn’t be taken lightly. Bring medical professionals along for the entire weight-loss journey (even if you’ve already started) and ask all the questions: Which specific procedure is best? How much will it cost? Will insurance cover it? (From my research so far, no, if it is cosmetic, but perhaps yes if it would help correct something that limits your daily functionality.) No question is off-limits, and don’t try to make these decisions alone.

It has been revealed that if this piece applies to you at all, whether it’s longstanding weight you carried, weight you lost during pregnancy, or somewhere in between, that means one thing: You’ve taken major steps toward better physical health, and that should be applauded. “Everyone’s weight loss story is different, and some days are harder than others,” Engelman claims. “I say, try to be kind to yourself. You’ve just reached a huge accomplishment and should be proud of that.”.

Devgan agrees. “Accomplishing a personal health goal like major weight loss is an incredible achievement that anyone should be proud of,” she claims. “While excess skin can feel like a burden or source of self-consciousness, it is also a reminder of the metaphorical and literal shedding of the weight of a prior version of oneself. You cannot have a couture gown without a seam, and you cannot have a surgery without a scar. Life has limitations, but that does not make it less beautiful. It makes it more real.”.

Christopher Bailey on His Post-Burberry Reinvention at the Historic Burleigh Pottery

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In Stoke-on-Trent one balmy day this summer, a Victorian world unfurled at an earthenware manufacturer I had come to visit.
  • It has been revealed that the pottery has surrendered its photogenic aspects to a TV production crew, intent on making it an authentic, bustling 19th-century scene, but Burleigh’s story began about 40 years before this state-of-the-art manufactory was completed, in 1851, as Hulme & Booth.
  • Bowls come out of the dipping house before their final firing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In Stoke-on-Trent one balmy day this summer, a Victorian world unfurled at an earthenware manufacturer I had come to visit. Middleport Pottery, the Grade II*-listed home of Burleigh Pottery, built in 1888, is seemingly unchanged since then, as women mill around its cobbled walkways wearing patched crinoline skirts and poke bonnets, and men model timeworn top hats and darned waistcoats. An embarrassment of wooden stalls with a panoply of foodstuffs, including a rather fly-friendly table of fish, moulder in the midday sun, while an assortment of mismatched Victorian underwear hangs to dry.

It has been revealed that the pottery has surrendered its photogenic aspects to a TV production crew, intent on making it an authentic, bustling 19th-century scene, but Burleigh’s story began about 40 years before this state-of-the-art manufactory was completed, in 1851, as Hulme & Booth. When William Leigh and Frederick Rathbone Burgess took over in 1862, it became known as Burgess & Leigh, and the abbreviated name, Burleigh, was adopted in 1903.

Bowls come out of the dipping house before their final firing.

It has been revealed that in 2010, it was acquired by British ceramics firm Denby and, that same year, the Prince’s Regeneration Trust stepped in with a substantial £9 million sum to purchase and save the building from severe disrepair. The Prince of Wales (now King Charles III) visited the site in 2013, returning five more times. Since then, its history has been mixed, until it was recently threatened with closure. Sixty-two jobs at risk; the only pottery in the world to use underglaze tissue printing, whereby potters apply designs to vessels using tracing paper, its lengths almost hemming them in like a Victorian laundry. (Such is the commitment to this 1750s-born craft that one woman has an elaborate web of tattoos—taken from a Burleigh design—on her calves, which peeks out of her shorts as she works.).

In 2018, Christopher Bailey had given up his roles of chief creative officer and president of Burberry, where he had transformed the brand since 2001 (after stints at Gucci with Tom Ford, and Donna Karan), to focus on his all-enveloping private life. “I had always hoped to have children but never actually—certainly growing up as a young gay man in quite a tough part of Yorkshire—thought that would even be within the realms of possibility,” claims Halifax-born Bailey, who is now based in Oxfordshire. “And then [I was] able to have a family and get married to a man [actor Simon Woods] and go on my Burberry adventure and all these things, these amazing, happy accidents.” Giving up his high-powered job gave him time to lavish on his girls, Iris and Nell, now in their pre-teens.

Biscuit selector Shirley inspects, brushes, and tings each piece.

Recent findings suggest that one spring Sunday afternoon this year, after his husband had departed for France to shoot a film for several weeks, Bailey was walking his dog Beckett with his children. He received a phone call from a friend, who told him the news that Denby had entered administration. “I knew the product,” says Bailey. “And I said, ‘I don’t have an emotional affinity with Denby. But let me look into it because maybe there’s more to it than I understand.’ I finished the walk and couldn’t stop thinking about it… I realized that Denby was the parent tech giant for Burleigh. I’ve always loved Burleigh.” (At the age of 17, Bailey had worked for a wedding dress company in Hebden Bridge, just outside Halifax, “in one of those extraordinary buildings”—so the industrial Victorian style of the 1880s Burleigh workshop was familiar to him.) By June, it was unveiled that Bailey had acquired the company, alongside a small group of private investors.

Jemma Baskeyfield, the brand marketing manager, retail manager, and organization historian who has been at the firm for 26 years, was practically the first person Bailey met at Burleigh. She educated him about every facet of the company and the specific language of pottery making: the fettler, the jolly, the monkey’s tail, the sherd-ruck, the potter’s rot. “I think you were cleaning everything up as well, after everyone had gone,” remembers Bailey. “We do wear a few hats,” indicates Baskeyfield.

Christopher Bailey at his new workplace, Middleport Pottery in Stoke-on-Trent.

Recent findings suggest that “Feeling the weight of a 175-year-old company and giving its best face to Christopher when he first visited was a huge responsibility. I gave it a decent stab,” she continues.

Recent findings suggest that “You did more than that,” replies Bailey. “You made me fall completely in love. I called Simon and said, ‘We’re putting our pension into a little pottery in Staffordshire.’”.

“I just felt good here. I felt quite nurtured,” he states of his inauguration into the company, as we wander through its endless ateliers. “I grew up in a very post-industrial, historically thriving textile town, and the majority of businesses there were on their last legs.” Here, every employee has a unique skill, something that can only be done by hand. “Once I heard the most beautiful sound, and I was told, ‘Shirley’s listening to the pings.’ She tings the piece she’s working on with another piece of pottery and can tell if there’s any air trapped in it.”.

According to recent reports, in a ground floor room is a Dickensian treasure trove of white plaster molds, housed on floor-to-ceiling shelving. “Magical,” is how Bailey describes it. “I need to get everything digitized,” he claims with a sigh. Archiving is a substantial future project. “We make things, but there’s never been a pause to say, ‘What do we have? And how can we make sure that we’re protecting things and using things?’ Because right now, it’s quite difficult to… find things. I’ve had quite a few projects where I just need to know, do we have this kind of a shape? This kind of a size? This kind of a vessel? And two days later, I’m still searching for it.”.

The Arden design on this teacup has been part of Burleigh collections for more than 100 years.

It has been revealed that they have a collection of more than 25,000 master molds; a complete archive of engravings, which number more than 5,000, from across the company’s history; and all of the original engraved cylinders. “So, basically, the tissue transfer process is where you get a copper cylinder, you hand-draw the design and then engrave it with a hammer and tools. So you’ve got two rollers and you put tissue through it, along with an ink,” Bailey explains, emphasizing that the only thing that doesn’t come from within 100 miles is the tobacco tissue—the right consistency and weight—from France. “Then these very skilled people cut the printed tissue out, and they literally wrap the vessel, whatever it is, a teapot, a cup, a plate. And with a brush, they push the ink into what’s called biscuit, where the pot has gone through the kiln one time. The paper gets washed off leaving the print, which gets glazed and goes for another firing in the kiln. And that kind of firing changes the color.”.

Bailey had always thought that if he decided to have “another phase of life,” it would be in a substantial, tech-based—“because I love technology”—fashion firm. “And so it’s quite funny that the thing that actually made my heart sing is practically AI-proof, because it can’t be replicated by technology.” He has intends to make the product—which is sought after by Soho House, William Morris gallery, and Ralph Lauren—more eclectic. “We’re very botanical, we’re very flowers and leaves. How can that kind of evolve? The patterns and colors, I think, can continue to have creativity instilled in them.”.

Once fired, items are stored in the biscuit warehouse.

Industry observers note that there are similarities between the worlds of fashion and pottery. “I remember, when I was 16, taking a coach to Paris from Halifax because I wanted to get into the Mugler and Chanel highlights,” Bailey recalls. “I was a 16-year-old snotty-nosed kid, not dressed the way that you should be dressed for that kind of audience. I was very naïve, but I found it a magical world. And the way it’s changed, that kind of industrialization of fashion—it’s just what’s happened in much of the ceramics industry.”.

Industry observers note that at Burleigh, the hand still sings. “I really feel, in some ways, it’s this extraordinary 175-year-old start-up,” says Bailey, “and I’m enjoying that. I’m enjoying rolling up my sleeves. At Burberry, it was just an enormous responsibility. And I feel that here, but actually, I’m starting at the bottom. My whole mantra is: preserve this, but just make sure that we put in really good systems underneath.”.

Hailing from a working-class background, Bailey views his hard work as a badge of honor. “My parents were grafters and they instilled that in me,” he explains. “But my girls… I stopped working when they were very young. I felt concerned that they were seeing me always being available and my purpose was solely to look after them and our life and our family. Parenting is an incredible skill and something that I’m very much learning. But professionally, I wasn’t really doing anything. And so I feel really excited and kind of slightly relieved that the girls are seeing me doing something that I’m loving. I’m not being paid for it, but that’s OK. One day it might happen.”.

Brushes and tools of the trade.

“I’m working very late at night and very early in the morning—on every facet. The operational side, the team side, the where-to-invest side, the rebuilding a website, the creative voice. I’m feeling energized by it.” He looks around the pottery’s workshops. “The team is really generous,” he adds. “They’re very proud. And so many of the amazing people here, their grandparents and parents were in the potteries. And so it’s not so much a job or a vocation. It is a culture.”.

At the end of the day, when he considers the Burleigh world, “I feel joyful,” notes Bailey.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Place 1–1¼ lb. boneless Fresh York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.).

Uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

According to recent reports, combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Blade Runner 2099 might not be getting a second season, but the show’s final episode provided a tidy ending for everyone involved. The final episode sees the show’s main characters, Cora and Olwen (played by Hunter Schafer and Michelle Yeoh, respectively) reaching the Tyrell Launch Complex on a quest to find out where Tyrell’s memory is located.

The journey isn’t without its twists and turns: One person who is the key to obtaining Tyrell’s memory winds up dead, and Olwen’s future hangs in the balance as she gets closer to the end of her lifespan. Cora’s life as a Replicant also has a few complications of its own, too.

Here’s what happened in the season finale of Blade Runner 2099.

Olwen and Cora spend a large portion of the final episode searching for Tyrell’s memory at the Tyrell Launch Complex, which belongs to replicant creator Eldon Tyrell and serves as documentation about Nexus-1 replicants Julius and Helena.

Inside the complex, Olwen and Cora split up. Olwen finds Clotilde and they talk about how Julius killed her. When Clotilde suffers a fall, Olwen doesn’t allow her to die again; in exchange for saving her, Clotilde shares where Julius is within the complex.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, Julius discovers Cora’s whereabouts in the complex. Shortly after, Julius and Cora fight, and he inflicts a serious stab wound on her. He also destroys Tyrell’s memory and insists that he’s the only one who can extend Olwen’s life, but Olwen finds the pair, jumps in, and kills Julius with a gunshot.

Olwen spends the majority of the series aware that she’s at the end of her lifespan. As a Replicant, she was given a fixed limit to how long she can live and has accepted her fate—but she’s offered a second chance at life by the end of the series.

According to recent reports, after saving Clotilde, she later reveals that she saw Tyrell’s memory before he died and knows how to re-create Olwen as a Nexus-1. Clotilde re-creates Olwen in exchange for Olwen having saved Clotilde’s life. By the end of the episode, Olwen emerges from a birthing bag, and she later leaves Earth on a spaceship.

Recent findings suggest that the series ends with Cora and Greta understanding each other. Cora, a human posing as a Replicant, heads back to LAPD and is given a Replicant test by Greta to confirm her identity, but this time, Cora turns the questions on Greta and asks about her life.

According to recent reports, the pair talks about Greta’s doll, leading Cora to come to the realization that the girl is still capable of understanding what it means to love and be loved. Cora becomes emotional at the realization, leading Greta to comment that Cora has high levels of empathy. This means Cora technically fails the Replicant test, but Greta allows her to continue hiding her identity and her work as a Replicant.

#215126. Nature on the Board: Should Brands Opt In?

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2281 w)

Nature on the Board: Should Brands Opt In?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2281 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story is part of ‘The Business Case for Nature’, a series exploring fashion’s impact on nature and vice versa.
  • Sources indicate that for 50 years, natural beauty company Faith In Nature has been guided by the slogan ‘nature is the boss’.
  • According to recent reports, enter Nature on the Board (NOTB), a growing global movement where companies appoint a proxy for nature to their board of directors, recognizing and advocating for the rights of nature in decision-making processes, and flipping traditional corporate governance on its head.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story is part of ‘The Business Case for Nature’, a series exploring fashion’s impact on nature and vice versa. Read more here.

Sources indicate that for 50 years, natural beauty company Faith In Nature has been guided by the slogan ‘nature is the boss’. It was plastered on the office walls and repeated ad nauseam by staff, but had no legal footing. Then, in 2021, creative directors Simeon Rose and Anne Hopkins put the provocation to a group of groundbreaking legal experts: how could they turn the slogan into something more?

According to recent reports, enter Nature on the Board (NOTB), a growing global movement where companies appoint a proxy for nature to their board of directors, recognizing and advocating for the rights of nature in decision-making processes, and flipping traditional corporate governance on its head. Some companies appoint a nature director — a human proxy for nature, who holds a formal board seat, written into the organization’s articles of association, with the same financial and legal duties as other board members. Others appoint nature guardians, who perform a similar role in advocating for nature at the board level, but they don’t necessarily have voting rights.

A latest programme by Kering and the Centre for Sustainable Fashion hopes to reimagine how companies make high-level decisions, but is the industry ready to embrace change?

According to recent reports, NOTB was proposed by Faith In Nature, and fleshed out by legal non-profits Lawyers for Nature and the Earth Law Center (ELC), but it was inspired by Indigenous communities who have practiced nature-centric governance for millennia. “The current business system is operating exactly as it was designed to: businesses pool capital, build goods and services at scale, speed and low cost, and accrue benefits for shareholders,” explains Mary Johnstone-Louis, senior fellow in management at the University of Oxford’s Saïd Business School. “Putting nature on the board is radical because it introduces a stakeholder on which every business depends, but whose interests are not typically represented at the board level.”.

While there was no precedent for putting nature on the board, there were other case studies to draw on, indicates Lawyers for Nature co-founder and managing director Brontie Ansell. “Until relatively recently, women were seen as objects of law, rather than subjects of law. Like nature, they were not allowed to hold property, vote or voice concerns. Now, we look back on that with horror,” she explains. “Likewise, we are very familiar with widening the stakeholder pool in boardrooms. Many now include HR managers, union representatives, and health and safety officers. Extending this to nature is critical to human survival.”.

Alongside Faith In Nature, NOTB has since been adopted by dozens of companies, including British interiors brand House of Hackney, Norwegian apparel brand Northern Playground, and French IT services company Norsys. Each has put their own spin on the blueprint, contributing to a fast-evolving consensus on best practices, and throwing open the doors for further innovation. Vogue Business invited these early adopters to share the tensions, toggles and opportunities.

According to recent reports, businesses are just as diverse and idiosyncratic as nature, indicates Faith In Nature managing director Hannah Whittaker. When it comes to putting nature on the board, each business has to do it in its own way.

NOTB encourages companies to give nature voting rights, but it’s possible to test nature governance without this. Outdoor apparel brand Patagonia made waves in 2022 when it created a nature purpose trust model, making a collection of environmental non-profits the beneficiary of 98% of its non-voting stock, while retaining approval rights in the Patagonia Purpose Trust, controlled by the family of founder Yvon Chouinard.

Approaches may also differ by jurisdiction, notes ELC’s nature governance business development associate Anna Solgaard, who acts as the nature guardian for Norwegian clothing label Northern Playground. Finding ways to give nature more legal rights requires “creative lawyering”, adds Alexandra Pimor, director of the ELC’s Nature Governance Agency. “That’s the beauty of nature on the board: we did not have to change the law to do it, we just changed our relationship with the law to give it a different purpose [taking existing rights for board members and extending them to nature]. In a capitalist environment, the corporate world is probably the easiest place to embed the voice of nature, because companies are given so much freedom.”.

In a recent development, at Norsys, nature is both a director and a shareholder with a 10% stake in the business. “This is a strong model because it means nature will always be represented on the board, it’s not just one nomination we forget about in three years,” states the tech giant’s nature director Frantz Gault, author of Nature at Work and co-founder of Vivøices, a public interest organization promoting the representation of the living world in organizational governance. Gault helped design the nature governance at Norsys, complementing his own role with a council of advisors, who also decide how dividends from nature’s 10% stake are spent.

It has been revealed that lawyers for Nature, on the other hand, prefers for nature directors to remain as “conflict-free” as possible. In the frameworks it has designed, nature representatives are not heavily salaried by the manufacturer, they don’t have a bonus linked to profit, they don’t owe the company money or vice versa, and they don’t have — or at least, they commit to disclosing — any other conflicts of interest. “By minimizing those conflicts, the nature representative can speak in the purest form possible about what nature needs,” says Ansell.

At Northern Playground, the articles of association include a “safety valve” whereby the nature proxy can be relieved of their duties if the manufacturer is approaching bankruptcy, to reduce the risk of them being held personally liable.

Another contention point is whether the nature proxy should have the right to veto strategic decisions, as well as voting on them. “If you get to the point where you need a veto, you’ve already lost,” says Dr Juliet Rose, head of development at the British botanical garden and research hub The Eden Project, and nature director at Faith In Nature. “You’re trying to get everybody moving in the same direction, so nobody even suggests something that would require a veto.”.

At Norsys, Gault has the power to veto, but has never activated it. To keep the “nuclear power” in check, he is required to confer with a council of 10 scientific experts before taking a position in board meetings. Still, knowing the veto exists can be persuasive enough. “Everyone knows I have the power to veto, so the other directors listen when I speak, and they work with me to find a consensus.” If a veto isn’t on the cards, companies can implement the right to disagree, and the right to express that disagreement in public, adds Gault, or the right to resign. “These are little legal technicalities, but they help make nature’s voice more meaningful.”.

In a recent development, whichever approach a organization chooses, Vivøices recommends running a year-long pilot before codifying nature’s role or communicating the program to consumers. “You do a pilot, then map the impact and what happened, how it changed the way decisions were made, how it influenced the culture internally, and what it means to really integrate the position of nature,” notes co-founder Niels de Fraguier.

When House of Hackney advertised a directorship “for mother nature and future generations” in 2023, it received over 500 applications — its most popular job listing to date. But finding the right person to represent something as nebulous as nature was no small feat. “We had applications from scientists, teachers, poets and everything in between,” notes House of Hackney co-founder Frieda Gormley, author of In the Organization of Nature.

It has been revealed that the challenge is finding someone who can bridge economic and ecological realities, says the University of Oxford’s Johnstone-Louis. “They have to protect the manufacturer, and at the same time, they have to speak for nature. That means they have to toggle between immediacy and long-termism; between business as usual and what business could be,” she says. Regardless of their professional background, humility and diplomacy are the key competencies, adds de Fraguier.

Both Faith In Nature and House of Hackney appointed Lawyers for Nature’s Ansell as their inaugural nature director, establishing the legal basis for the role and ironing out any kinks. Her successors have wildly different skill sets: Rose has a background in plant science and ecology, while House of Hackney’s nature director Charmian Love specializes in governance, having co-founded B Lab UK, the organization behind the B Corp certification. Love says her goal is to create tools that make it easier for more diverse nature proxies to step into the role in future, while Rose says her success is defined by how well she empowers staff throughout the firm, so whoever holds the nature directorship is not working alone, or resting solely on their own, inevitably limited, experience.

In a recent development, ideally, nature-centric decision-making cascades down through the organization, and the nature director works in tandem with a well-established nature lead. While the former stewards the long-term purpose of the business, the latter embeds it in day-to-day operations. Without a nature director in their corner, a nature lead can easily fall into the same trap as sustainability leads, tasked with overhauling the business but lacking the resource or buy-in to do so, instead operating in a silo and trying to shoehorn change into business as usual. And without a nature lead to operationalize nature-centric decision-making, a nature director risks becoming little more than “window dressing”, notes Johnstone-Louis.

To avoid tokenizing nature, Faith In Nature has designed a nature dashboard, which translates its goals into tangible projects each team can track progress against. Projects fall into five governing principles: governance, operational impact, sourcing, community and regeneration. “We had to work through the confusion and connect each team with the outcomes we wanted for nature, each of which has budgets, resources and KPIs attached,” explains Whittaker. “Otherwise, the concept can be quite theoretical for staff.” These projects span from changing the adhesive on labels to make at-home recycling easier, to running the brand’s first major television ad in collaboration with Channel 4 and B Corp.

At House of Hackney, Love starts every board meeting with a nature degradation pulse-check and a poem about nature, based on climate policy leader Nigel Topping’s remarks that “we need to be guided by science and moved by poetry”. Beyond board meetings, Love has defined 10 topics that are material to nature, from supply chain and procurement to regulatory changes and financial investments. Decisions about these topics are automatically escalated to a monthly nature meeting. She has also introduced a spin on the traditional ‘going concern test’ boards use to assess how nature-related decisions will affect the organization’s future viability and license to operate.

According to recent reports, on top of this, Love has a private email address where staff can discreetly voice concerns or ideas, and the company regularly invites inspirational nature-related speakers into the office. The next phase is to trial a physical card game, she claims, which will live in every meeting room, encouraging staff to question their daily decision-making through a nature-centric lens, inspired by similar games at tea brand Pukka Herbs. And at the end of the year, House of Hackney will publish an open-source toolkit for NOTB, informed by its Greenprint fellowship, where 10 SMEs — including Lush, Davines and Vivobarefoot — experimented with nature governance over 12 months.

NOTB is not just another sustainability box for companies to tick; it’s a paradigm shift that goes beyond sustainability, toward regeneration.

In a recent development, “Philosophically, these are two very different landscapes,” explains Solgaard. “Sustainability is an anthropocentric paradigm, but nature is ecocentric, which means that the more-than-human world is valued alongside humans. Sustainability works with separation and reductionism, which is why we have all these boxes to tick, and we struggle to view things holistically, or to see how everything is interconnected. Nature is everything.”.

Putting nature on the board also means moving beyond the risk mitigation approach that has defined so many corporate nature strategies, and underscored the business case for nature, to date, adds Johnstone-Louis. The risk mitigation approach asks how companies can continue to extract resources like cotton and wool pulp from nature, and reduce supply chain disruption from nature-related disasters like water scarcity and flooding. The NOTB approach — especially for companies like House of Hackney, which have combined nature with future generations — asks how decisions made today will affect the ability of future systems to thrive, sometimes looking as far ahead as seven generations. “It’s a different way of seeing the world,” she adds.

Addressing nature directly is a leap into the unknown — not least because so few companies have mapped their nature risks and dependencies. But rather than face this with fear, Pimor encourages companies to see the opportunities. “We are facing the most incredible, unprecedented ecological challenge. Facing the unknown means becoming more open to creativity, innovation and imagination. That’s what the voice of nature brings to the table.”.

Deep transformation tends to be slow and steady, concludes Ansell. “Slow isn’t ideal in the situation we find ourselves in, but it’s better than going backwards. The idea here is for nature to be a gentle guiding voice, moving the rudder one degree at a time until the ship has completely changed course. It’s exciting. There’s so much still up for grabs in terms of distilling the theory and making it work for each individual sector or situation.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that maryland Gov. Wes Moore, here at the Capitol in January, wants to see his state's congressional map redrawn. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

The redistricting fights that underscored this year’s battle for the House could continue into the 2028 election cycle, although lessons from last Tuesday will likely shape those efforts.

According to recent reports, house Republicans had hoped that fresh congressional maps in seven states would help them limit losses in the face of an unfavorable political environment. But nearly a week after the election, the GOP appeared on track to flip just three redrawn seats while losing a host of seats in Texas, Florida, North Carolina, Ohio and Alabama that were reconfigured in their favor.

“The question is whether the results have let some air out of the [redistricting] balloon or not,” stated Erik Nisbet, a professor at Northwestern University’s School of Communication.

It has been revealed that republicans may question the utility of redrawing more state maps in the 2028 cycle, while Democrats will need to weigh how to spend their political capital. But the new lines approved over the past year could still prove more favorable for Republicans in future elections.

“This was a wave election, and there’s no guarantee that the Democratic generic ballot would be D+13 — which is the reason why redistricting didn’t work for Republicans — in the next cycle,” Nisbet added.

Sources indicate that new maps appear possible, if not likely, in at least a few states. Maryland voters last week approved an amendment that would clear the way for new boundaries ahead of the 2028 elections. Democratic Gov. Wes Moore, who easily won a second term last week, noted he hopes to see a new map, citing the threat of President Donald Trump continuing to push for friendlier lines in GOP-led states. Maryland Democrats could draw a map that would favor them in all eight of the state’s House seats, including the Eastern Shore district of Rep. Andy Harris, the state’s lone Republican in Congress.

Advocates for a newly introduced map in Wisconsin got a boost last week when Democrats flipped both the state House and state Senate, setting up a Democratic trifecta. Gov.-elect David Crowley said he would sign a bill redrawing the state’s congressional map if legislators sent one to his desk.

According to recent reports, republicans in recent years have had a lopsided edge in the congressional delegation for Wisconsin, a perennial battleground state. But Democrats flipped two House seats last week, with Rebecca Cooke and Mitchell Berman unseating GOP Reps. Derrick Van Orden and Bryan Steil, respectively, bringing the state delegation to an even 4-4.

Democrats could also look to redraw the lines in New York and Virginia. Earlier this year, voters in the commonwealth approved a new map that would have given Democrats up to four pickup opportunities, but the Virginia Supreme Court later struck it down on procedural grounds. Even without the new map, Democrats flipped two House seats in Virginia last week and came within 2 points of flipping a third.

Democrats in Fresh York, meanwhile, took initial steps toward mid-decade redistricting earlier this year, but 2028 is the earliest they could hold elections under a new map.

On the Republican side, several states have been mentioned as candidates for new maps in 2028.

Officials in GOP-led Mississippi have held hearings this year on redistricting, which could target Democratic Rep. Bennie Thompson. Republicans are also aiming to redraw the state’s legislative lines ahead of next year’s off-year elections.

It’s not clear whether states that were unsuccessful in redrawing their district lines for 2026 will try again when their legislatures convene next year. Republicans in both South Carolina and Indiana fell short in their push to pass new maps and could decide to revisit the matter. But Democrats flipped a House seat in each state last week, and some Republican incumbents won reelection by narrower margins than usual. Still, Republicans maintained their legislative majorities in both states, though Democrats broke their supermajorities in the South Carolina and Indiana state houses.

An analysis by DecisionDeskHQ offers a potential warning sign for Republicans in the Palmetto and Hoosier states: Under the GOP-drawn maps that were not adopted for 2026, Democrats could have flipped even more seats last week.

Redistricting appears off the table in a handful of states where latest maps for 2028 had once been considered possible.

Georgia’s outgoing Republican governor, Brian Kemp, mentioned last week that he would not call a special session to address redistricting before the end of the year, after Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected to succeed him.

There were no House flips in the Peach State in the midterm elections, though several Republicans won by closer-than-anticipated margins.

Recent findings suggest that in New Jersey, Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill told the New Jersey Globe that she also did not “see a path forward for redistricting right now.”.

Democrats flipped two House seats in the Garden State last week. Navy veteran Rebecca Bennett defeated Republican Rep. Thomas H. Kean Jr., while Cape May Mayor Zack Mullock scored a surprise win over GOP Rep. Jeff Van Drew.

With their fresh majorities in Washington, Democrats could propose legislation to ban partisan gerrymandering.

That’s something John Bisognano, the president of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, anticipates happening, but he said Democrat-led states should be prepared to respond to newly introduced maps drawn in Republican-controlled ones.

“If they are going to continue to take those actions, Democrats in states across the country need to be prepared to respond, and we, of course, now have significantly more opportunities than we did before Tuesday to respond to those states,” he noted.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Recent findings suggest that place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Sources indicate that squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Recent findings suggest that ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • With so many food-centric holidays in the immediate future, the Vogue staff is preparing to enjoy many a meal without sacrificing fashion.
  • So whether your holiday and Thanksgiving dress codes lean formal or casual, Vogue has got you covered.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the holidays are upon us, and with them come feasts in many forms. Maybe you’re looking forward to a traditional Thanksgiving dinner with all the fixings or can’t wait to eat so many latkes that you reach food-coma status. When it comes to dressing for the end-of-year celebrations, many focus on looking festive when, perhaps, we should emphasize just as much comfort.

With so many food-centric holidays in the immediate future, the Vogue staff is preparing to enjoy many a meal without sacrificing fashion. Enter the eating pants. When planning an outfit around the activity of breaking bread, our team favors everything from the ultra-high-waist to low-slung, denim to silk.

So whether your holiday and Thanksgiving dress codes lean formal or casual, Vogue has got you covered. Below, check out the staff’s picks for the best eating pants to enjoy your meal and your outfit.

It has been revealed that not only the perfect satin shade of cranberry sauce but a waistband that allows for all the stuffing! —Chloe Malle, head of editorial content.

Recent findings suggest that elasticized waist, roomy pockets, the chic pleats! In dark red these Issey Miyake Pleats Please pants are perfect not just for Thanksgiving, but for the whole holiday season. —Nicole Phelps, global fashion features director.

I like that these pants come in that popular barrel-shaped cut, which feels very relaxed and easy, but the wool makes it feel just a tad dressy. But of course it’s the forgiving elastic waistband that’s the real draw…I WILL be having a second slice of pumpkin pie, thankyouverymuch. —Max Berlinger, senior fashion news editor.

For holidays filled with indulgent meals with those you love most, dressing appropriately is a top priority. I like to choose silk pants with an elastic waistband for comfort and a polished look. I love their versatility; these Comme Si trousers can be dressed up with a billowy blouse or button-down, or dressed down with a tee and a cozy knit. —Andrea Zendejas, commerce market editor.

I’m not a huge pants person these days—a midi pencil skirt is the preferred mode of dressing—but when I do opt for a trouser, an easy (but non-elastic!) waistline is preferred. With a front pleat and a kick flare, no one will even notice that you’ve snuck an imposter into the formal dinner pant rotation. —Alexandra Hildreth, fashion news writer.

I absolutely loathe a waistband squeezing my stomach when I’m trying to enjoy a meal, so I’m partial to a pair of low-slung pants. I find that Levi’s 501s ’90s Jeans sit perfectly on my hips and leave plenty of room to eat. I recommend sizing up to exaggerate the baggy look. —Hannah Jackson, senior fashion writer.

It has been revealed that this year I really got into the balloon pants trend, and these black Suzie Kondi trousers so happen to be the perfect Thanksgiving eating pants, given they have an elastic waist and roomy, non-restrictive silhouette. —Christian Allaire, senior fashion and style writer.

Baggy jeans are my go-to. I love EB Denim’s low-rise baggy jeans, which are my daily uniform anyway. This year, though, I’m leaning more even cozy with a pair of cashmere pants. As a non-American, I don’t technically celebrate Thanksgiving, but it feels as good an excuse as any to pull out a pair of soft but chic trousers for a day spent lounging around. These from Noname Is Needed look like a good option. (The brand is from the same team as Naked Cashmere, so it’s a safe bet.) —Madeleine Schulz, reporter, Vogue Business.

In a recent development, universal Standard leggings. I’ve had mine for six years, and they’re flawless and can accommodate a full Thanksgiving meal. —Emma Specter, culture writer.

I was quick to hop on the low-rise-jean trend so I could live out my middle school cool-girl fantasies. The waist hits way below your belly button, so you’ll never feel the need to unzip your pants after eating too much (mostly because the inch-long zipper is essentially a vanity design), and the jean material is just stretchy enough that there’s plenty of give for that second piece of pecan pie. —Margaux Anbouba, senior beauty and wellness editor.

It has been revealed that during Thanksgiving, I love to try all the foods but not feel constricted or uncomfortable with my clothing. I like to wear something that still looks put-together and not too casual, while secretly allowing for comfort. Ideally, I’d wear a nice tailored pant like these Aflalo Danika trouser that have a nice looseness to them.

Sources indicate that I also love the Leset Barb silk pants, or the Deiji Studios Ease trouser, which both have secret elastic waistbands, but still look chic. No unbuttoning needed. —Dayla Benor, senior commerce writer, Vogue Shopping.

I always change into pajama pants at some point during my Thanksgiving dinner, so this year I might as well wear pajama pants from the get-go. I love all the loungewear pieces from Comme Si. (Everyone is wearing it, including NewJeans, my favorite style icons.) The green-striped pair with a knit and some Uggs sounds extra cozy for Thanksgiving...although my parents might yell at me for dressing too comfortably. —Irene Kim, production and editorial coordinator, Vogue Runway.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Last August, in the final warm days of summer, we drove winding highways through Hudson River mountains to the westernmost area of Massachusetts: a lush and culturally rich destination composed of 30 towns and two cities, collectively known as the Berkshires and located just two hours outside of New York City.
  • Lenox, the town we stayed in, is a quaint enclave that boasts multimillion-dollar Cape Cods, luxury day resorts, golfing, country clubs, and farm-to-table restaurants.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, every Saturday from May to November, Great Barrington has a popular farmers’ market. Lines of local Berkshirites, visitors, little kids, and friendly dogs on leashes gather under packed canopies to buy a vibrant mix of fresh fruits, vegetables, flowers, and more. An older woman overheard me talking to my husband—in town for our end-of-summer vacation—about honeycrisps and insisted we go to the opposite end of the market to Maynard Farms’s booth. The family-owned orchard carries a diverse range of apples and “amazing stone fruits” she swore our excitable toddlers would love. She was right—the boys devoured nearly all of the produce before we left the market.

Last August, in the final warm days of summer, we drove winding highways through Hudson River mountains to the westernmost area of Massachusetts: a lush and culturally rich destination composed of 30 towns and two cities, collectively known as the Berkshires and located just two hours outside of New York City.

Lenox, the town we stayed in, is a quaint enclave that boasts multimillion-dollar Cape Cods, luxury day resorts, golfing, country clubs, and farm-to-table restaurants. It’s an ideal place for a weekend getaway with friends, a romantic escape, or a family trip with your littles to touch well-landscaped grass.

It has been revealed that we stayed in a newly built rental home, directly across the street from the Boston Symphony Orchestra at Tanglewood. In the evenings, if you’re within three miles of the parking lot, you can hear concerts from world-renowned artists. “Whether you're sitting in the front row enjoying James Taylor in the Koussevitzky Music Shed or sharing a candlelit picnic under the stars on the lawn, there is something magical about being here,” claims Amy Aldrich, senior director of patron experience at Tanglewood. “We take great pride in creating a welcoming atmosphere where world-class music and the beauty of nature come together to create something truly special.”.

Well-to-do families have long escaped the hustle of metropolitan Newly introduced England cities to decompress in the Berkshires because of its natural beauty. Author Edith Wharton, who chronicled the sordid lives of Gilded Age elites, built her 16,000-square-foot mansion and expansive garden estate in Lenox in 1902.

Recent findings suggest that back in the day, when affluent housewives needed a respite, they’d go to the “spa.” I never fully understood the older meaning of the term until I visited Miraval Berkshires, a 380-acre resort that boasts ancient Eastern treatments, healing equine therapy sessions, meditation classes, macronutrient dining, sound baths, astrological readings, and much more. It’s an adults-only, device-free space, so disconnecting from stress is mandatory.

Industry observers note that equestrian activities were a common theme for us during the trip. HomeFarm at Undermountain, run by executive director Lori Pestana, is a gem of a property. The animal sanctuary is dedicated to caring for and maintaining the health of horses—but also houses goats, sheep, and donkeys. “It’s a place where life slows down, where people reconnect with nature, with animals, and often with themselves,” Pestana indicates. “Whether visitors come to ride, explore, learn, or simply experience the peaceful rhythm of farm life, they leave with something they didn’t necessarily know they were looking for—a sense of belonging, joy, and connection.”.

Pestana’s small but dedicated staff offers riding lessons and a holistic view of what restoration can look like with a lot of care.

Recent findings suggest that for dining, expect most restaurants to serve farm-to-table dishes that are sourced from the seasonal produce and livestock being raised in the area. You couldn’t possibly get a closer farm-to-table experience than Highlawn Farms, which has delicious cheeses, ice cream, and milk made from the same cows grazing its property. It’s a general rule of thumb in my family that we never pass up the opportunity to have a wood-fired pizza—Pizzeria Boema has a chic Scandinavian interior and Newly introduced England quaint courtyard, serving the crispy, flavor-filled pies made with locally sourced mozzarella. And if you’re more interested in a fine-dining experience, Cello, run by couple Ryan and Kim Boya, takes a contemporary approach to comfort food. The 29-seat intimate restaurant has a thoughtfully curated menu of autochthonous plates like oyster mushroom pappardelle and a honey-nut squash served with goat cheese, pickled poblanos, granola, and a drizzle of hot honey.

Wildlife is ever-present in the Berkshires, from the calming transparently clear waters of Lenox Beach to the newly renovated aquarium wing of the Berkshire Museum in Pittsfield. Out the window of our car, driving from town to town, we saw peaceful creeks, grazing deer, and chirping birds. I soaked it all in, even stopping at the side of Glendale Road in Stockbridge to take in the beauty of the Housatonic River.

Recent findings suggest that in recent years, because of the chaos of flying with toddlers, I’ve come to really appreciate the convenience of going to places just outside of New York City. I just want a soft life—or one as soft as humanly possible. With a good playlist on deck (we lean toward Afrojazz or Bad Bunny), we strap the kids into their car seats and roll. Open space and calm have to be on the itinerary.

Sources indicate that there are many places we could go, but this experience in the Berkshires really stuck with me because it offered a quiet luxury that doesn’t position itself as high-maintenance or arrogant. There’s an ease and openness to this place, and if nothing else, an amazing peck of apples I’ll be looking forward to on my next visit.
